challenges.title: Does God exist?
challenges.summary: The world is ordered and not self-made. That is a reason to trust the God who gave it being.
challenges.source: Basil the Great, Hexaemeron, Homily 1, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, volume 8

lessons.heading: A world that did not invent itself
lessons.body:
Christians do not pretend that a sentence can drag God into a laboratory. We do say the world is a poor candidate for “it just happened.” Things that begin, change, and fall apart do not explain why there is anything at all. A mind that finds order, beauty, and reliable laws in that world is already meeting a gift, not a closed machine.

Basil the Great, preaching on Genesis, refuses the guess that the world assembled itself: “I am about to speak of the creation of heaven and earth, which was not spontaneous, as some have imagined, but drew its origin from God.” Paul says the same from the other direction: “The invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead” (Romans 1:20).

Science can tell how a star burns. It does not, by counting the burning, answer who gave the star a place to burn. The Church’s first answer is not a trick. It is worship: the world is creature, and God is the one who was already there.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: The existence of God is not a spare part added to a world that already explains itself. The world points past itself. Basil’s line is enough to keep: creation drew its origin from God, and it was not spontaneous.

questions.prompt: What does Basil deny about the origin of heaven and earth?
choices: That they can be studied at all
That they came to be spontaneously, without God
That God is distinct from the world
questions.explanation: In the Hexaemeron Basil says the creation of heaven and earth was not spontaneous, but drew its origin from God.

questions.prompt: Romans 1:20 says God’s eternal power and Godhead are clearly seen by what?
choices: A private feeling with no link to the world
The things that are made
A vote of the nations
questions.explanation: Paul says the invisible things of God are understood by the things that are made.

challenges.summaryEs: El mundo tiene orden y no se hizo solo. Eso es una razón para confiar en el Dios que le dio el ser.

lessonsEs.heading: Un mundo que no se inventó solo
lessonsEs.body:
Los cristianos no fingimos que una frase puede meter a Dios en un laboratorio. Sí decimos que el mundo es un mal candidato para “así nomás pasó”. Lo que empieza, cambia y se deshace no explica por qué hay algo en vez de nada. Una mente que encuentra orden, belleza y leyes confiables en ese mundo ya está recibiendo un regalo, no una máquina cerrada.

Basilio el Grande, predicando sobre Génesis, rechaza la idea de que el mundo se armó solo: “Voy a hablar de la creación del cielo y de la tierra, que no fue espontánea, como algunos imaginaron, sino que tuvo su origen en Dios”. Pablo dice lo mismo desde el otro lado: “Porque las cosas invisibles de él, su eterna potencia y divinidad, se echan de ver desde la creación del mundo, siendo entendidas por las cosas que son hechas” (Romanos 1:20, RV1909).

La ciencia puede decir cómo arde una estrella. Contar ese fuego no responde quién le dio un lugar para arder. La primera respuesta de la Iglesia no es un truco. Es adoración: el mundo es criatura, y Dios es el que ya estaba ahí.

challenges.title: Why the Trinity?
challenges.summary: The Church names one God, not three gods, because the Father, the Son, and the Spirit have been shown together.
challenges.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 40.41, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, volume 7

lessons.heading: One God, not a committee
lessons.body:
A common objection says that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must mean three gods. That would be true if “Person” meant “a separate being with a separate divine nature.” The Church says the opposite. There is one divine nature. The Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, and they are not three Gods side by side, and not one Person wearing three masks.

The Scriptures already speak this way before the later word “Trinity” was used as a summary. At the Jordan the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. The risen Christ sends the Church to baptize “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Matthew 28:19). One name, three Persons.

Gregory of Nazianzus keeps the mind from splitting what God has joined: “No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the Splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One.” The Father is the source. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father. The Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father. That is not three origins of three gods. It is the one God as he has made himself known.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: The Trinity is not a puzzle invented to confuse outsiders. It is the Church refusing two mistakes: collapsing the Persons into one mask, and dividing the one God into three gods.

questions.prompt: Gregory says that as soon as he conceives of the One, he is illumined by what?
choices: A fourth divine person
The splendour of the Three
The idea that the Persons are only names
questions.explanation: Gregory’s Oration 40 says the thought of the One is illumined by the Splendour of the Three, and the distinction of the Three returns him to the One.

questions.prompt: Which sentence matches the baptismal confession?
choices: Three gods share a project
One God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, not three gods and not one Person in costume
Only the Father is divine, and the Son is a creature
questions.explanation: Matthew 28:19 names the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in one name. The Church confesses one divine nature and three Persons.

challenges.summaryEs: Un solo Dios, y el Hijo y el Espíritu no son creaciones tardías. La Escritura habla de los tres sin dividir al único Dios.

lessonsEs.heading: Un solo Dios, no un comité
lessonsEs.body:
Una objeción común dice que Padre, Hijo y Espíritu Santo tienen que significar tres dioses. Eso sería cierto si “Persona” quisiera decir “un ser aparte, con una naturaleza divina aparte”. La Iglesia dice lo contrario. Hay una sola naturaleza divina. El Padre es Dios, el Hijo es Dios, el Espíritu es Dios, y no son tres Dioses uno al lado del otro, ni una sola Persona con tres máscaras.

Las Escrituras ya hablan así, antes de que la palabra “Trinidad” se usara como resumen. En el Jordán el Hijo es bautizado, el Espíritu desciende y el Padre habla. El Cristo resucitado envía a la Iglesia a bautizar “en el nombre del Padre, y del Hijo, y del Espíritu Santo” (Mateo 28:19). Un solo nombre, tres Personas.

Gregorio Nacianceno no deja que la mente parta lo que Dios ha unido: “Apenas concibo al Uno, y ya me ilumina el resplandor de los Tres; apenas los distingo, y ya me veo llevado de vuelta al Uno”. El Padre es la fuente. El Hijo es engendrado eternamente del Padre. El Espíritu procede eternamente del Padre. Eso no son tres orígenes de tres dioses. Es el único Dios tal como se ha dado a conocer.

challenges.title: The Resurrection: what is the evidence?
challenges.summary: Paul hands on a burial, a third day, and named witnesses. The Church began from that claim.
challenges.source: 1 Corinthians 15, in the King James text read in this app

lessons.heading: A claim with names on it
lessons.body:
The Resurrection is not a mood the disciples later felt about Jesus. Paul passes on what he had received: “Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: and that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve” (1 Corinthians 15:3–5). He goes on to the five hundred, to James, to all the apostles, and last to himself.

Notice what is included. A death. A burial. A day. Names. This is the sort of claim that can be checked by people who were alive, and contradicted by people who were also alive. The Gospels add that the first witnesses at the tomb were women. In that world a story invented to sound impressive would not have started there.

The other piece of evidence is the Church herself. The same men who hid became the men who preached a crucified and risen Lord in the city where he had been killed. They did not preach “his cause lives on.” They preached that the tomb was empty and that they had seen him.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: The apostolic claim is bodily and public: buried, raised, and seen. A “spiritual meaning only” reading has to erase the burial, the third day, and the witnesses Paul lists.

questions.prompt: In 1 Corinthians 15, what does Paul say he delivered?
choices: A private symbol with no witnesses
What he also received: Christ’s death, burial, resurrection, and appearances
That Jesus never really died
questions.explanation: Paul says he delivered what he received: Christ died, was buried, rose the third day, and was seen.

questions.prompt: Why does the women’s witness matter in this argument?
choices: It proves the Gospels were written centuries later
It is an unlikely detail for a story polished to impress that culture
It means the apostles never claimed to see him
questions.explanation: The first witnesses at the tomb being women is a stubborn detail. It does not fit a legend designed to sound officially impressive.

challenges.summaryEs: Los relatos no suenan a un rumor pulido. Empieza por lo que dicen los testigos y por la tumba vacía.

lessonsEs.heading: Un anuncio con nombres
lessonsEs.body:
La resurrección no es un estado de ánimo que los discípulos sintieron después acerca de Jesús. Pablo transmite lo que había recibido: “Que Cristo fué muerto por nuestros pecados, conforme á las Escrituras; y que fué sepultado, y que resucitó al tercer día, conforme á las Escrituras; y que apareció á Cefas, y después á los doce” (1 Corintios 15:3–5). Sigue con los quinientos, con Jacobo, con todos los apóstoles y, al final, consigo mismo.

Fíjate en lo que incluye. Una muerte. Una sepultura. Un día. Nombres. Es el tipo de anuncio que pueden revisar personas que estaban vivas, y que también pueden contradecir personas que estaban vivas. Los Evangelios añaden que las primeras testigos del sepulcro fueron mujeres. En aquel mundo, un relato inventado para sonar impresionante no habría empezado por ahí.

La otra pieza de evidencia es la Iglesia misma. Los mismos hombres que se escondieron se volvieron los que predicaban a un Señor crucificado y resucitado en la ciudad donde lo habían matado. No predicaban “su causa sigue viva”. Predicaban que el sepulcro estaba vacío y que lo habían visto.

challenges.title: Are the Gospels reliable?
challenges.summary: Luke ties his book to eyewitnesses. Irenaeus ties the four Gospels to the apostles’ preaching.
challenges.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1

lessons.heading: Preaching that was written down
lessons.body:
A Gospel is not a modern biography, and it is not a fog of legends from centuries later. Luke tells Theophilus that he is writing “of those things which are most surely believed among us, even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word” (Luke 1:1–2). He expects his reader to recognize a tradition already being handed on.

Irenaeus, late in the second century, still names the living link. “Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, did also hand down to us in writing what had been preached by Peter. Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him.” He says Matthew wrote for the Hebrews, and that John, “the disciple of the Lord,” published his Gospel at Ephesus. You do not have to treat every detail of that report as a modern footnote to see the point: the churches knew these books as apostolic preaching, while the preaching could still be compared with the communities that had received it.

Reliability here does not mean the four books are photocopies of one another. John is not Mark. It means they are early, traceable, and received by the Church as the apostolic witness to one Lord.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: The Gospels stand inside a Church that could still name who preached them. They are the apostles’ witness written down, not anonymous myths invented after everyone who could object was dead.

questions.prompt: Irenaeus says Mark wrote down the preaching of whom?
choices: Peter
A philosopher who never met the apostles
A council that met in the Middle Ages
questions.explanation: Against Heresies 3.1.1 calls Mark the disciple and interpreter of Peter, and says he wrote what Peter had preached.

questions.prompt: Luke 1 says the tradition he writes down came from whom?
choices: Eyewitnesses and ministers of the word
People who never claimed to have seen Jesus
A single unsigned scroll found centuries later
questions.explanation: Luke says the things he records were delivered by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word.

challenges.summaryEs: Cuatro relatos cercanos a los hechos, con nombres, lugares y detalles que un invento tardío no necesita.

lessonsEs.heading: Predicación que se puso por escrito
lessonsEs.body:
Un Evangelio no es una biografía moderna, ni una niebla de leyendas de siglos después. Lucas le dice a Teófilo que escribe “la historia de las cosas que entre nosotros han sido ciertísimas, como nos lo enseñaron los que desde el principio lo vieron por sus ojos, y fueron ministros de la palabra” (Lucas 1:1–2). Espera que quien lo lee reconozca una tradición que ya se estaba transmitiendo.

Ireneo, a fines del siglo II, todavía nombra el eslabón vivo. “Marcos, discípulo e intérprete de Pedro, también nos transmitió por escrito lo que Pedro había predicado. Lucas, compañero de Pablo, registró en un libro el Evangelio predicado por él”. Dice que Mateo escribió para los hebreos, y que Juan, “el discípulo del Señor”, publicó su Evangelio en Éfeso. No hace falta tratar cada detalle de ese informe como una nota al pie moderna para ver el punto: las iglesias conocían estos libros como predicación apostólica, mientras esa predicación todavía podía compararse con las comunidades que la habían recibido.

Confiabilidad aquí no significa que los cuatro libros sean copias uno del otro. Juan no es Marcos. Significa que son tempranos, que se les puede seguir el rastro, y que la Iglesia los recibió como el testimonio apostólico de un solo Señor.

challenges.title: Why is there evil and suffering?
challenges.summary: God is not the author of evil. The Cross is God’s answer from inside suffering, not a shrug.
challenges.source: James 1:13 and the passion of Christ, in the King James text read in this app

lessons.heading: God is not the author of the wound
lessons.body:
The hardest objection is not a clever one. It is a hospital room. If God is good and strong, why this pain? The Church refuses two easy exits. Evil is not a second god equal to the Holy Trinity. And evil is not a tool God needed in order to be interesting. James is blunt: “Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man” (James 1:13).

What God made, he called good. A person made in his image can turn a good gift against the Giver. That turning is not a substance. It is a misuse, and it spreads: death, cruelty, a world at odds with itself. The fall is that wound. It does not make God the craftsman of cancer and war.

The Christian answer is not a diagram that makes the wound feel tidy. It is Christ. The Son takes flesh, weeps at a grave, and enters death itself. The Resurrection does not call suffering a illusion. It says death does not get the last word over the world God still loves.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: Do not charge God with being the source of evil. Evil is the ruin of what he made good. His answer is not distance. It is the incarnate Son, who suffers with us and breaks death.

questions.prompt: James 1:13 forbids which sentence?
choices: God can be tempted with evil, and he tempts us
God is good
Christ entered death
questions.explanation: James says God cannot be tempted with evil, and he does not tempt anyone. Do not say the temptation came from God.

questions.prompt: Which reply matches this lesson?
choices: Evil is a second god, equal to the Father
Suffering is not real
God does not author evil; in Christ he enters suffering and overcomes death
questions.explanation: The lesson refuses both a second evil god and a denial of pain. The Cross and Resurrection are God’s way with the wound.

challenges.summaryEs: La Escritura no esconde el dolor. Tampoco lo llama el plan secreto de Dios para lastimar.

lessonsEs.heading: Dios no es el autor de la herida
lessonsEs.body:
La objeción más dura no es una objeción ingeniosa. Es una habitación de hospital. Si Dios es bueno y fuerte, ¿por qué este dolor? La Iglesia se niega a dos salidas fáciles. El mal no es un segundo dios igual a la Santísima Trinidad. Y el mal no es una herramienta que Dios necesitara para resultar interesante. Santiago es directo: “Cuando alguno es tentado, no diga que es tentado de Dios: porque Dios no puede ser tentado de los malos, ni él tienta á alguno” (Santiago 1:13).

Lo que Dios hizo, lo llamó bueno. Una persona hecha a su imagen puede volver un buen regalo contra quien lo da. Ese giro no es una sustancia. Es un mal uso, y se extiende: muerte, crueldad, un mundo en discordia consigo mismo. La caída es esa herida. No convierte a Dios en el artesano del cáncer y de la guerra.

La respuesta cristiana no es un diagrama que deje la herida ordenadita. Es Cristo. El Hijo toma carne, llora ante una tumba y entra en la muerte misma. La resurrección no llama al sufrimiento una ilusión. Dice que la muerte no tiene la última palabra sobre el mundo que Dios todavía ama.

challenges.title: Why Church Tradition?
challenges.summary: The apostles handed on the faith by living speech and by letter. Basil says both have force.
challenges.source: Basil the Great, On the Holy Spirit 27.66, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, volume 8

lessons.heading: Handed on, not invented later
lessons.body:
“Tradition” sounds, to some ears, like a rumor that competes with the Bible. In the Church it means the handing on of the apostolic faith: the Gospel preached, the Scriptures read in the assembly, baptism, the Eucharist, the sign of the cross, the way the Church prays. Paul tells the Thessalonians to “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Word and letter belong together.

Basil the Great says the same in the fourth century: “Of the beliefs and practices whether generally accepted or publicly enjoined which are preserved in the Church some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force.” He is not licensing anyone to invent a new gospel. He is saying the Church did not receive a naked book and a blank life. She received a way.

Scripture is not embarrassed by that. Scripture itself tells the Church to hold what was taught aloud. Tradition, rightly named, is Scripture’s own home, not a rival canon of private opinions.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: Tradition is the apostolic faith being handed on, in writing and in the Church’s life. Basil says those two do not cancel each other. They have the same force for true religion.

questions.prompt: Basil says written teaching and apostolic tradition stand how?
choices: Tradition cancels Scripture
Both have the same force in relation to true religion
Only customs invented after the apostles matter
questions.explanation: On the Holy Spirit 27.66 says what comes from written teaching and what was delivered in a mystery by apostolic tradition have the same force.

questions.prompt: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 says to hold the traditions taught in which ways?
choices: By word, or by epistle
By private guesswork only
By ignoring what the apostles said aloud
questions.explanation: Paul says to hold the traditions taught whether by word or by his epistle.

lessonsEs.heading: Entregada, no inventada después
lessonsEs.body:
“Tradición”, para algunos oídos, suena a un rumor que compite con la Biblia. En la Iglesia significa la transmisión de la fe apostólica: el Evangelio predicado, las Escrituras leídas en la asamblea, el bautismo, la Eucaristía, la señal de la cruz, el modo en que la Iglesia ora. Pablo les dice a los tesalonicenses: “estad firmes, y retened la doctrina que habéis aprendido, sea por palabra, ó por carta nuestra” (2 Tesalonicenses 2:15). La palabra hablada y la carta van juntas.

Basilio el Grande dice lo mismo en el siglo IV: “De las creencias y prácticas, ya aceptadas en general o mandadas en público, que se conservan en la Iglesia, unas las tenemos derivadas de la enseñanza escrita; otras las hemos recibido entregadas en misterio por la tradición de los apóstoles; y ambas, en lo que toca a la verdadera religión, tienen la misma fuerza”. No le está dando permiso a nadie para inventar un evangelio nuevo. Está diciendo que la Iglesia no recibió un libro pelado y una vida en blanco. Recibió un camino.

La Escritura no se avergüenza de eso. La Escritura misma le dice a la Iglesia que retenga lo que se enseñó en voz alta. La Tradición, bien nombrada, es la casa propia de la Escritura, no un canon rival de opiniones privadas.

challenges.title: Why icons are not idolatry
challenges.summary: Christ really became visible. Honour given before his icon is meant for him, not for the paint.
challenges.source: John of Damascus, An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 4.16, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, volume 9

lessons.heading: The honour does not stop at the wood
lessons.body:
Israel was forbidden to bow to a statue and call it the invisible God. That command still stands. What changed is the Incarnation. “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The invisible Son became a man who could be seen. To picture him is to confess that this really happened. A faith that forbids every image of Christ is in danger of treating his humanity as an idea instead of a life.

John of Damascus, in the public-domain Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, is plain about what the gesture means. Seeing the image of the crucifixion, “we fall down and worship not the material but that which is imaged: just as we do not worship the material of which the Gospels are made.” And: “the honour rendered to the image passes over to the prototype.” The older English says “worship” for the bow. The point of his sentences is the opposite of idolatry. Paint is not God. The honour crosses the paint and belongs to Christ.

So an icon is a form of witness, like a Gospel book you can see. We kiss the Gospel book without believing the leather is a god. We venerate an icon without offering the adoration that belongs to the Holy Trinity alone.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: Icons are not idols. Idolatry treats the made thing as God. An icon of Christ sends the honour to Christ, because the Word truly took a face.

questions.prompt: John of Damascus says the honour rendered to the image passes where?
choices: It stops in the paint, which is itself divine
It passes over to the prototype, the person shown
It is forbidden because Christ was never visible
questions.explanation: He says the honour rendered to the image passes over to the prototype, and that we do not worship the material.

questions.prompt: Which comparison does he make?
choices: An icon is unlike a Gospel book, because only the icon is adored as wood
We do not worship the material of an image, just as we do not worship the material of the Gospels
The Incarnation made images unnecessary
questions.explanation: He compares the image with the Gospel book: the honour is for what they present, not for leather or paint as God.

lessonsEs.heading: El honor no se queda en la madera
lessonsEs.body:
A Israel se le prohibió inclinarse ante una estatua y llamarla el Dios invisible. Ese mandamiento sigue en pie. Lo que cambió es la Encarnación. “Y aquel Verbo fué hecho carne, y habitó entre nosotros” (Juan 1:14). El Hijo invisible se hizo un hombre que se podía ver. Retratarlo es confesar que esto de verdad ocurrió. Una fe que prohíbe toda imagen de Cristo corre el peligro de tratar su humanidad como una idea, en vez de una vida.

Juan Damasceno, en la Exposición de la fe ortodoxa, es claro sobre lo que significa el gesto. Al ver la imagen de la crucifixión, “nos postramos y adoramos no la materia, sino aquello que está representado: así como no adoramos la materia de la que están hechos los Evangelios”. Y: “el honor que se rinde a la imagen pasa al prototipo”. La palabra antigua con la que él nombra la inclinación a veces se ha vertido como adoración. El punto de sus frases es lo contrario de la idolatría. La pintura no es Dios. El honor cruza la pintura y le pertenece a Cristo.

Así, un ícono es una forma de testimonio, como un libro de los Evangelios que puedes ver. Besamos el Evangelio sin creer que el cuero es un dios. Veneramos un ícono sin ofrecer la adoración que pertenece solo a la Santísima Trinidad.

challenges.title: Why we honor the Theotokos and the saints
challenges.summary: Mary is called Mother of God because of who her Child is. The saints are alive in Christ and pray.
challenges.source: Cyril of Alexandria to Nestorius, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, volume 14; John of Damascus, Orthodox Faith 4.16

lessons.heading: Honour that refers back to Christ
lessons.body:
Mary says, “From henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). The Church does. The title Theotokos, Mother of God, is not a claim that Mary existed before God or that she is a fourth person of the Trinity. Cyril of Alexandria writes why the Fathers used it: “not as if the nature of the Word or his divinity had its beginning from the Holy Virgin, but because of her was born that holy body with a rational soul, to which the Word being personally united is said to be born according to the flesh.” The title protects Jesus. The one in her womb is the eternal Son, not a mere man later adopted.

John of Damascus draws the line for her honour and for the saints: “the honour which we give to her is referred to Him Who was made of her incarnate.” The brave acts of holy people “stir us up to be brave and to emulate and imitate their valour and to glorify God.” We ask them to pray because death does not cut the Church in half. James already says to “pray one for another” (James 5:16). If the prayer of a righteous person matters here, it matters in the kingdom.

None of this puts Mary or a saint in the place of the Trinity. We do not offer them the adoration due to God alone. We honor what Christ has done in them, and we ask their prayers.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: Theotokos means the Child is God incarnate, not that Mary is the source of the divine nature. Honour given to her and to the saints is meant to glorify Christ, and their prayers do not replace his.

questions.prompt: Why does Cyril say the Virgin is called Mother of God?
choices: Because the divine nature began from her
Because the body born of her is personally united to the Word
Because she is a fourth divine person
questions.explanation: Cyril denies that the Word’s divinity began from Mary. She is called Mother of God because the Word was personally united to the body born of her.

questions.prompt: John of Damascus says the honour we give Mary is referred to whom?
choices: To her instead of Christ
To him who was made incarnate of her
To the paint of an icon as a god
questions.explanation: He says the honour given to her is referred to him who was made of her incarnate, and that the saints’ lives move us to glorify God.

lessonsEs.heading: Un honor que vuelve a Cristo
lessonsEs.body:
María dice: “desde ahora me dirán bienaventurada todas las generaciones” (Lucas 1:48). La Iglesia lo hace. El título Teotokos, Madre de Dios, no afirma que María existiera antes que Dios ni que sea una cuarta persona de la Trinidad. Cirilo de Alejandría escribe por qué los Padres lo usaron: “no como si la naturaleza del Verbo o su divinidad hubiera tenido su principio en la santa Virgen, sino porque de ella nació aquel cuerpo santo, con alma racional, al cual el Verbo, unido personalmente, se dice nacido según la carne”. El título protege a Jesús. El que está en su vientre es el Hijo eterno, no un simple hombre adoptado después.

Juan Damasceno traza la línea para el honor de ella y de los santos: “el honor que le damos se refiere a Aquel que de ella se hizo carne”. Los actos valientes de las personas santas “nos animan a ser valientes, a emular e imitar su valor y a glorificar a Dios”. Les pedimos que oren porque la muerte no parte a la Iglesia en dos. Santiago ya dice: “rogad los unos por los otros” (Santiago 5:16). Si la oración de una persona justa importa aquí, importa en el reino.

Nada de esto pone a María o a un santo en el lugar de la Trinidad. No les ofrecemos la adoración que se debe solo a Dios. Honramos lo que Cristo ha hecho en ellos, y pedimos sus oraciones.

challenges.title: Why the Church, and not the Bible alone?
challenges.summary: The Church preached before she bound the New Testament. Scripture is her book, not a rival to her.
challenges.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.4.1, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1

lessons.heading: The book was received somewhere
lessons.body:
“Bible alone” still has to answer a prior question: which books, read by whom, with which baptismal faith? The New Testament did not fall from the sky already bound. The apostles preached, baptized, and broke bread. Letters and Gospels were written inside that life, and the Church recognized them. Paul calls “the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). He does not call a private reader that pillar.

Irenaeus presses the point. “For how should it be if the apostles themselves had not left us writings? Would it not be necessary to follow the course of the tradition which they handed down to those to whom they did commit the Churches?” Even with the writings, he will not separate the books from the churches that received the apostles’ teaching.

So the Orthodox answer is not “the Church instead of Scripture.” It is that Scripture is the Church’s apostolic book, read in the Church’s faith. A verse yanked free of that faith can be made to say almost anything. The same Spirit who inspired the writings gathered a people to guard them.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: The Bible is not a rival to the Church that received it. Without the Church there is no canon, no baptism, and no living place where the apostolic word is heard as one faith.

questions.prompt: Irenaeus asks what believers would follow if the apostles had left no writings. His answer is:
choices: Each person’s newest opinion
The tradition handed down to the churches the apostles committed
No faith at all until a printing press
questions.explanation: Against Heresies 3.4.1 says it would be necessary to follow the tradition handed down to those to whom the apostles committed the Churches.

questions.prompt: 1 Timothy 3:15 calls the Church what?
choices: The pillar and ground of the truth

A later invention with no link to the apostles
questions.explanation: Paul calls the church of the living God the pillar and ground of the truth.

lessonsEs.heading: El libro se recibió en algún lugar
lessonsEs.body:
“Solo la Biblia” todavía tiene que responder una pregunta anterior: ¿qué libros, leídos por quién, con qué fe bautismal? El Nuevo Testamento no cayó del cielo ya encuadernado. Los apóstoles predicaron, bautizaron y partieron el pan. Las cartas y los Evangelios se escribieron dentro de esa vida, y la Iglesia los reconoció. Pablo llama a “la iglesia del Dios vivo, columna y apoyo de la verdad” (1 Timoteo 3:15). No llama columna a un lector privado.

Ireneo aprieta el punto. “Pues, ¿qué sería si los mismos apóstoles no nos hubieran dejado escritos? ¿No sería necesario seguir el curso de la tradición que ellos entregaron a aquellos a quienes encomendaron las Iglesias?” Aun con los escritos, no separa los libros de las iglesias que recibieron la enseñanza de los apóstoles.

Así que la respuesta ortodoxa no es “la Iglesia en vez de la Escritura”. Es que la Escritura es el libro apostólico de la Iglesia, leído en la fe de la Iglesia. Un versículo arrancado de esa fe se puede hacer decir casi cualquier cosa. El mismo Espíritu que inspiró los escritos reunió a un pueblo para guardarlos.

challenges.title: The Eucharist is the real Body and Blood
challenges.summary: Christ said “this is my body.” Ignatius says the Eucharist is the flesh of the Saviour.
challenges.source: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Smyrnaeans 7, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1

lessons.heading: Not a bare reminder
lessons.body:
At the supper, Jesus “took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26). In John 6 he says, “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.” The Church did not hear this as poetry for a feeling. She heard a gift.

Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom early in the second century, already treats a merely symbolic view as a refusal of Christ. Some, he says, “abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again.” The same flesh that suffered and rose is the flesh he says the Eucharist is.

The Liturgy does not pretend the bread stops looking like bread. It confesses a change we do not see: by the Holy Spirit, the gifts become the Body and Blood of Christ. We do not re-sacrifice him. We receive the one sacrifice, and we adore Christ present, not the wheat as wheat.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: The Orthodox Church receives the Eucharist as Christ’s true Body and Blood. Ignatius already called a refusal of that confession a turning away from the gift.

questions.prompt: Ignatius says some abstain from the Eucharist because they will not confess it to be what?
choices: An ordinary meal with no link to Christ
The flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered and was raised
A symbol that Christ is absent
questions.explanation: To the Smyrnaeans 7 says they do not confess the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour, which suffered and which the Father raised.

questions.prompt: Which sentence fits this lesson?
choices: Christ meant the supper only as a memory that he is absent
The Church offers a second, separate sacrifice of a different Christ
The one sacrifice is received as his real Body and Blood
questions.explanation: The lesson confesses a real presence and the one sacrifice, not a bare symbol and not a second Christ.

lessonsEs.heading: No es un mero recordatorio
lessonsEs.body:
En la cena, Jesús “tomó el pan, y bendijo, y lo partió, y dió á sus discípulos, y dijo: Tomad, comed: esto es mi cuerpo” (Mateo 26:26). En Juan 6 dice: “Si no comiereis la carne del Hijo del hombre, y bebiereis su sangre, no tendréis vida en vosotros”. La Iglesia no oyó esto como poesía para un sentimiento. Oyó un don.

Ignacio de Antioquía, camino al martirio a principios del siglo II, ya trata una visión meramente simbólica como un rechazo de Cristo. Algunos, dice, “se abstienen de la Eucaristía y de la oración, porque no confiesan que la Eucaristía es la carne de nuestro Salvador Jesucristo, la que padeció por nuestros pecados, y a la que el Padre, por su bondad, resucitó”. La misma carne que padeció y resucitó es la carne que él dice que es la Eucaristía.

La Liturgia no finge que el pan deje de verse como pan. Confiesa un cambio que no vemos: por el Espíritu Santo, los dones se vuelven el Cuerpo y la Sangre de Cristo. No lo volvemos a sacrificar. Recibimos el único sacrificio, y adoramos a Cristo presente, no al trigo como trigo.

challenges.title: Faith and science
challenges.summary: Creation can be studied because God made an ordered world. That study does not replace the Maker.
challenges.source: Basil the Great, Hexaemeron, Homily 1, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, volume 8

lessons.heading: Two questions, one world
lessons.body:
The Church does not ask you to despise the patient study of creation. Basil wants the hearer “eager to find in its surroundings an idea of God which may be worthy of Him,” and he denies that heaven and earth were “spontaneous.” A world that came from God is a world with order in it. Measuring that order is not atheism. It is looking at a work.

Trouble starts when either side grabs the other’s question. Science, in its ordinary work, asks how things behave: what a cell does, how old a rock is, which cause follows which. It does not, by weighing and timing, settle whether the whole show is a gift, whether a person is only a machine, or whether the dead are raised. Faith does not hand out lab results by quoting Genesis as if it were that kind of manual. Faith says who the Maker is, what a human being is for, and where the world is going.

When a Christian fears a telescope, or a scientist announces that a method has abolished God, both have changed the subject. The Orthodox posture is calmer. Study the world honestly. Do not pretend the study was the Creator.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: Faith and science are not rival gods. Science describes the creation. The Church confesses the God who gave it being. Confuse the questions, and you will invent a war the Gospel did not start.

questions.prompt: Basil wants the student of creation to be eager for what?
choices: An idea of God worthy of God, found in the things around us
A proof that the world had no origin
A ban on asking how the world works
questions.explanation: In the Hexaemeron he urges a soul eager to find in its surroundings an idea of God worthy of him, and he denies a spontaneous world.

questions.prompt: Which distinction does this lesson draw?
choices: Science replaces the question of why there is a world at all
A description of how things behave does not by itself answer who gave them being
Faith is only useful where measurement has failed
questions.explanation: The lesson says scientific description and the confession of the Creator answer different questions about the same world.

challenges.summaryEs: Estudiar cómo funciona el mundo no compite con adorar a quien lo hizo.

lessonsEs.heading: Dos preguntas, un solo mundo
lessonsEs.body:
La Iglesia no te pide que desprecies el estudio paciente de la creación. Basilio quiere que quien escucha esté “deseoso de hallar en lo que lo rodea una idea de Dios que sea digna de él”, y niega que el cielo y la tierra hayan sido espontáneos. Un mundo que vino de Dios es un mundo con orden dentro. Medir ese orden no es ateísmo. Es mirar una obra.

El problema empieza cuando un lado le arrebata la pregunta al otro. La ciencia, en su trabajo ordinario, pregunta cómo se comportan las cosas: qué hace una célula, qué edad tiene una roca, qué causa sigue a cuál. Por pesar y medir el tiempo no resuelve si todo el conjunto es un regalo, si una persona es solo una máquina, o si los muertos resucitan. La fe no reparte resultados de laboratorio citando Génesis como si fuera ese tipo de manual. La fe dice quién es el Hacedor, para qué es un ser humano y hacia dónde va el mundo.

Cuando un cristiano le teme a un telescopio, o un científico anuncia que un método ha abolido a Dios, los dos han cambiado de tema. La postura ortodoxa es más serena. Estudia el mundo con honestidad. No finjas que el estudio era el Creador.

challenges.title: Why miracles?
challenges.summary: A miracle is God acting freely in the world he made. The Resurrection is the one that interprets the rest.
challenges.source: John of Damascus, An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 4.16, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, volume 9

lessons.heading: Signs, not magic
lessons.body:
A miracle is not a stunt that breaks a world God has abandoned. It is the Lord of the world acting freely in it: a healing, a storm rebuked, bread in the wilderness, and above all a dead man raised. The point is not to skip faith. John says the signs he records were written “that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (John 20:31).

John of Damascus ties the wonders to history, not to a fog. The Lord “worked miracles, suffered, was crucified, rose again,” and “since all these things actually took place and were seen by men, they were written for the remembrance and instruction of us who were not alive at that time.” The Church does not ask you to believe in “miracles in general” as a mood. She asks you to believe this Lord, whose greatest sign is the Resurrection.

That also sorts counterfeits. A wonder that leads away from Christ, or that treats God as a vending machine, is not the Gospel’s kind of sign. The true ones serve the kingdom. They show that death and sickness are not the owners of the world.

lessons.heading: Takeaway
lessons.body: Miracles are God acting in his own creation, witnessed and then told. The Resurrection is the miracle that tells you what the others mean.

questions.prompt: John of Damascus says the miracles, the passion, and the resurrection were what?
choices: Events that took place, were seen, and were written down for those who came later
Legends with no witnesses
Proof that the material world is an illusion
questions.explanation: He says these things actually took place and were seen, and were written for the instruction of those who were not there.

questions.prompt: John 20:31 says the signs were written so that the reader might what?
choices: Believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God
Treat God as a machine that owes us wonders
Stop caring whether Christ rose
questions.explanation: John says these things are written that you might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.

challenges.summaryEs: Un milagro no es un truco contra las leyes. Es el Creador actuando en lo que él mismo hizo.

lessonsEs.heading: Señales, no magia
lessonsEs.body:
Un milagro no es una acrobacia que rompe un mundo que Dios ha abandonado. Es el Señor del mundo actuando con libertad en él: una sanación, una tormenta reprendida, pan en el desierto y, sobre todo, un muerto resucitado. El punto no es saltarse la fe. Juan dice que las señales que registra se escribieron “para que creáis que Jesús es el Cristo, el Hijo de Dios” (Juan 20:31).

Juan Damasceno ata las maravillas a la historia, no a una niebla. El Señor “hizo milagros, padeció, fue crucificado, resucitó”, y “como todas estas cosas sucedieron de verdad y fueron vistas por los hombres, se escribieron para memoria e instrucción de nosotros, que no estábamos vivos en aquel tiempo”. La Iglesia no te pide que creas en “los milagros en general” como un estado de ánimo. Te pide que creas en este Señor, cuya mayor señal es la resurrección.

Eso también ordena las falsificaciones. Una maravilla que aparta de Cristo, o que trata a Dios como una máquina expendedora, no es el tipo de señal del Evangelio. Las verdaderas sirven al reino. Muestran que la muerte y la enfermedad no son las dueñas del mundo.

challenges.title: The one God and the three Persons
challenges.summary: Distinguish nature from person, then test what the Creed actually protects.
challenges.source: OCA · The Holy Trinity

questions.prompt: What does the Nicene claim that the Son is of one essence with the Father deny?
choices: That the Father and Son are distinct Persons
That the Son is a creature of a different nature
That the Son became human
That God created the world
questions.explanation: The Nicene confession that the Son is of one essence with the Father denies that the Son is a creature of a different nature; it does not deny that Father and Son are distinct Persons.

questions.prompt: A friend says the Father, Son, and Spirit are simply three masks one Person wears. What is the problem?
choices: It divides the one divine nature
It denies the real distinction of the three Persons
It says God has no will
It makes the Son too human
questions.explanation: Three masks worn by one Person is modalism: it denies the real, eternal distinction of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: How many divine natures does Orthodox Trinitarian teaching confess?
choices: One
Two
Three
None
questions.explanation: Orthodox teaching confesses one divine nature, or essence, shared fully by the three Persons.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best avoids both tritheism and modalism?
choices: Three gods cooperate
One Person changes roles
Three distinct Persons share one divine nature
The Spirit is an impersonal power
questions.explanation: Three distinct Persons sharing one divine nature avoids both tritheism, which would make three gods, and modalism, which would make the Persons mere roles.

questions.prompt: Why does theology of the Trinity matter for Christian life?
choices: It replaces prayer with definitions
Communion with God is life in the Father through the Son in the Spirit
It proves humans become God by nature
It makes love optional
questions.explanation: Trinitarian doctrine matters because salvation and prayer are communion with the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, not because definitions replace prayer.

challenges.titleEs: El único Dios y las tres Personas
challenges.summaryEs: El Padre, el Hijo y el Espíritu son un solo Dios, no tres dioses ni tres modos de hablar.

questionsEs.prompt: ¿Qué niega la afirmación nicena de que el Hijo es de una sola esencia con el Padre?

lessons.heading: The cross
lessons.body: The Cross was an instrument of death. In Christ’s hands it became the instrument of salvation. St Basil connects the “sign of the Son of Man” at the Second Coming with the arms of the Cross: the Cross is not only a past event but the sign under which the Lord returns. Christians sign themselves with it, bless with it, and are guarded by it in travel, work, sleep, and prayer. It ties the Old Testament to the New, and the New to the age to come, when material signs will no longer be needed because God will be all in all. Until then, the Cross is how the Church touches that victory in the body.

lessonsEs.heading: La cruz
lessonsEs.body: La cruz fue un instrumento de muerte. En las manos de Cristo se volvió el instrumento de la salvación. San Basilio une la “señal del Hijo del hombre” en la segunda venida con los brazos de la cruz: la cruz no es solo un hecho del pasado, sino la señal bajo la cual el Señor regresa. Los cristianos se santiguan con ella, bendicen con ella y son guardados por ella en el viaje, el trabajo, el sueño y la oración. Ata el Antiguo Testamento con el Nuevo, y el Nuevo con el siglo venidero, cuando los signos materiales ya no harán falta porque Dios será todas las cosas en todos. Hasta entonces, la cruz es el modo en que la Iglesia toca esa victoria en el cuerpo.

challenges.title: The case that Jesus is God
challenges.summary: Build a cumulative case from John, Paul, Hebrews, and the resurrection.
challenges.source: OCA · The Incarnation

lessons.heading: Start with the claim, not a slogan
lessons.body: Orthodoxy does not say Jesus is the Father. It says the one Jesus Christ is the eternal Son, personally distinct from the Father, sharing the divine nature and truly assuming a complete human nature. John 1:1 and 1:14 hold together distinction, divinity, and incarnation.

lessons.heading: Read John in its own sequence
lessons.body: John 1:1–3 puts the Word before created things, describes him as with God and as God, and says all things came to be through him. John 1:14 identifies that Word as the one who became flesh. John 20:28 records Thomas addressing the risen Jesus as “My Lord and my God.” John 17:3 records Jesus addressing the Father as the only true God. The Orthodox reading does not discard the last text; it distinguishes the Father from the Son without making the Son a creature.

lessons.heading: Read worship and divine identity together
lessons.body: Philippians 2:6–11 moves from Christ’s divine status through humiliation to his exaltation and universal confession as Lord, echoing Isaiah 45:23. Hebrews 1:8–12 addresses the Son with language of divine kingship and creation; its use of Psalm 102 warrants close reading in context. Colossians 1:16–17 and 2:9 present all creation in relation to him and the fullness of deity dwelling bodily in him. A cumulative argument is stronger than relying on a single ambiguous word.

lessons.heading: Handle the hard texts honestly
lessons.body: Jesus prays, learns, suffers, and says the Father is greater (John 14:28). These are genuine data, not verses to hide. The Incarnation means the Son acts and speaks in a real human life; passages of dependence must be read alongside texts of preexistence and divine identity. The argument requires a theological synthesis; it is not a mathematical proof forced by one verse.

lessons.heading: The Christ of the Gospels: God and man
lessons.body: In the Gospels the same Jesus is shown as God and as man in one life. He is born as children are born, and yet not from a human father: from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. He hungers, sleeps, weeps, and asks, and the same narratives have Him forgive sins, command the sea, and rise. Do not divide the portrait into a human half and a divine half kept in separate chapters. The Church reads one Lord whose human actions carry the divine imprint, and whose divine works are done in a real human life.

challenges.title: Proving the Trinity responsibly
challenges.summary: One God, distinct Father, Son, and Spirit: build the case without a bad analogy.
challenges.source: OCA · The Three Divine Persons

lessons.heading: Define the terms first
lessons.body: “One” answers what God is: the one divine nature. “Three” answers who: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The claim is not that one Person is three Persons, or that one nature is three natures. Analogies such as water changing states easily collapse the real distinction of Persons and are not proofs.

lessons.heading: Keep the Shema
lessons.body: Deuteronomy 6:4 confesses the Lord as one, and Jesus affirms the commandment in Mark 12:29. Trinitarian faith does not add gods to Israel’s God. Its question is how Jesus and the Spirit are spoken of within the worship and action of the one God. A Jewish reader can disagree with the Christian answer without being accused of denying the Shema.

lessons.heading: Follow the narrative
lessons.body: At Jesus’s baptism (Matthew 3:16–17), the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. In Matthew 28:19, baptism is into the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. John 14–16 speaks of the Son asking the Father to send the Paraclete. These texts support personal distinction; other texts establish the Son’s and Spirit’s divine life and action.

lessons.heading: Respect the limits of “proof”
lessons.body: The word “Trinity” is a later theological term. The developed vocabulary is not printed as a single New Testament sentence. The Christian case is an inference from multiple passages and the Church’s worship: one God, the Son’s divine identity, the Spirit’s personal divine action, and distinction among them. A serious defense explains each premise and its rival readings.

lessons.heading: How to explain the mystery of the Holy Trinity
lessons.body: The catechism tells two old stories of St Spyridon at Nicaea, and both refuse to turn the Trinity into a puzzle you solve. In one, he presses a brick and speaks of fire and water in the one clay: an image of three in one, not a mechanism. In the other, a shepherd stops a long argument with a philosopher and says, in effect: God is one, the Creator, who made all things by the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son became incarnate, died, and rose. Do not labor for evidence of what faith alone can receive. Answer instead: do you believe in the Son of God? The Trinity is the One to whom we pray, and also the communion of three in whose image human community is meant to be built. Explanation serves prayer. It does not replace it.

lessonsEs.heading: Define primero los términos
lessonsEs.body: “Uno” responde qué es Dios: la única naturaleza divina. “Tres” responde quién: Padre, Hijo y Espíritu Santo. La afirmación no es que una Persona sea tres Personas, ni que una naturaleza sea tres naturalezas. Analogías como el agua que cambia de estado disuelven con facilidad la distinción real de las Personas, y no son pruebas.

lessonsEs.heading: Conserva el Shemá
lessonsEs.body: Deuteronomio 6:4 confiesa: “Oye, Israel: Jehová nuestro Dios, Jehová uno es”, y Jesús afirma el mandamiento en Marcos 12:29. La fe trinitaria no le añade dioses al Dios de Israel. Su pregunta es cómo se habla de Jesús y del Espíritu dentro de la adoración y la acción del único Dios. Un lector judío puede no estar de acuerdo con la respuesta cristiana sin que se lo acuse de negar el Shemá.

lessonsEs.heading: Sigue el relato
lessonsEs.body: En el bautismo de Jesús (Mateo 3:16–17), el Hijo es bautizado, el Espíritu desciende y el Padre habla. En Mateo 28:19, el bautismo es en el nombre singular del Padre, del Hijo y del Espíritu Santo. Juan 14–16 habla del Hijo pidiendo al Padre que envíe al Paráclito. Estos textos sostienen la distinción personal; otros textos establecen la vida y la acción divinas del Hijo y del Espíritu.

lessonsEs.heading: Respeta los límites de la “prueba”
lessonsEs.body: La palabra “Trinidad” es un término teológico posterior. El vocabulario desarrollado no está impreso como una sola frase del Nuevo Testamento. El caso cristiano es una inferencia a partir de varios pasajes y del culto de la Iglesia: un solo Dios, la identidad divina del Hijo, la acción divina personal del Espíritu, y la distinción entre ellos. Una defensa seria explica cada premisa y las lecturas rivales.

lessonsEs.heading: Cómo explicar el misterio de la Santísima Trinidad
lessonsEs.body: El catecismo cuenta dos historias antiguas de san Espiridón en Nicea, y las dos se niegan a convertir la Trinidad en un acertijo que tú resuelves. En una, aprieta un ladrillo y habla del fuego y del agua en la misma arcilla: una imagen de tres en uno, no un mecanismo. En la otra, un pastor detiene una discusión larga con un filósofo y dice, en sustancia: Dios es uno, el Creador, que hizo todas las cosas por el Hijo y el Espíritu Santo; el Hijo se encarnó, murió y resucitó. No te afanes por evidencias de lo que solo la fe puede recibir. Responde más bien: ¿crees en el Hijo de Dios? La Trinidad es el Uno a quien oramos, y también la comunión de tres a cuya imagen se ha de construir la comunidad humana. La explicación sirve a la oración. No la reemplaza.

challenges.title: Why the councils mattered
challenges.summary: Trace which question each council faced and what its answer did and did not say.
challenges.source: OCA · The Councils

lessons.heading: Nicaea I (325) and Constantinople I (381)
lessons.body: Nicaea I rejected the claim that the Son was made from nothing and confessed him of one essence with the Father. Constantinople I reaffirmed Nicene faith and defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Neither council claimed the Father and Son are one Person.

lessons.heading: Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451)
lessons.body: Ephesus insisted that Mary is Theotokos because the one she bore is the divine Son incarnate. Chalcedon confessed one and the same Christ in two complete natures, without confusion or division. “Two natures” is not “two Sons”; “one Person” does not erase his full humanity.

lessons.heading: Constantinople III (680–681) and Nicaea II (787)
lessons.body: The Sixth Council affirmed Christ’s divine and human wills, in accord with his two natures, without rivalry. Nicaea II defended icons and distinguished veneration from worship of God alone, tied to the reality of the Incarnation. Each decision addresses a different consequence of confessing the Word made flesh.

lessons.heading: Read councils as interpretive judgments
lessons.body: Councils did not create Jesus’s divinity by vote or add a new member to the Trinity. They used philosophical vocabulary to rule out interpretations they judged incompatible with apostolic faith. History still matters: ask which dispute a formula answered, what text was at stake, and where Christians outside Eastern Orthodoxy contest its reception.

challenges.title: Comparing religious objections fairly
challenges.summary: Engage Muslim, Jewish, and Jehovah’s Witness objections without misrepresenting their beliefs.
challenges.source: OCA · Trinity and Incarnation

lessons.heading: First understand the actual objection
lessons.body: The Qur’an 4:171 rejects saying “Trinity” and describes Jesus as a messenger; 5:72 rejects identifying the Messiah with God. Christian and Muslim readings thus differ at the identity of Jesus and the meaning of divine unity. Do not tell a Muslim that the Trinity is Father, Mary, and Jesus, or that divine begetting is physical. Those are not Orthodox claims.

lessons.heading: Jewish monotheism is a real disagreement
lessons.body: Traditional Jewish belief strongly affirms God’s unique, indivisible oneness and rejects Christian claims about Jesus. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is central for both Jewish and Christian discussion. A Christian argument cannot simply assume that every Jewish use of “Lord” already means a Trinity; it must explain its reading of the New Testament and Israel’s Scriptures while admitting the other reading.

lessons.heading: Nontrinitarian Christian readings
lessons.body: Jehovah’s Witnesses reject the Trinity and distinguish Jesus from Almighty God, often appealing to John 17:3 and the Father’s primacy. Orthodoxy agrees that Father and Son are personally distinct but argues from John 1, John 20:28, Philippians 2, and Hebrews 1 that the Son is uncreated and truly divine. Discuss actual passages and translation choices rather than merely declaring the other side dishonest.

lessons.heading: What counts as a good case?
lessons.body: State the other position in terms its adherents recognize. Present a cumulative case, handle the strongest countertext, distinguish a historical fact from a theological interpretation, and say what your evidence cannot compel. “Proving” in apologetics means giving a reasoned defense, not pretending that disagreement disappears.

questions.explanation: Mary is not a divine member of the Trinity; that is a misrepresentation of Orthodox belief.

questions.explanation: A fair start affirms God’s oneness in the Shema and then explains the distinct Christian claim about Jesus.

questions.explanation: John 17:3, where Jesus calls the Father the only true God, is a direct objection that should be engaged rather than avoided.

questions.explanation: Orthodox sonship is an eternal relation, not physical procreation by God.

questions.explanation: A cumulative argument should present a coherent case and answer rival interpretations honestly, not claim one verse ends all disagreement.

lessonsEs.heading: Primero entiende la objeción real
lessonsEs.body: El Corán 4:171 rechaza decir “Trinidad” y describe a Jesús como un mensajero; 5:72 rechaza identificar al Mesías con Dios. Así, las lecturas cristiana y musulmana difieren en la identidad de Jesús y en el sentido de la unidad divina. No le digas a un musulmán que la Trinidad es Padre, María y Jesús, ni que el engendrar divino es físico. Esas no son afirmaciones ortodoxas.

El Shemá (Deuteronomio 6:4) es central para la conversación judía y para la cristiana. challenges.title: The Islamic Dilemma
challenges.summary: The Quran affirms the Bible — and disagrees with it. Learn the two horns and the one question that opens the conversation.
challenges.source: The Quran · the early manuscripts · St. John of Damascus

lessons.heading: The setup: the Quran points to the Bible
lessons.body: The Quran calls the Torah and the Gospel God's revealed books. It tells Jews to judge by the Torah and Christians by the Gospel (Q 5:43-47), tells Muhammad, if he is in doubt, to ask those who read the Scripture before him (Q 10:94), and insists no one can change the words of God (Q 6:115; 18:27). On its own terms, then, the Bible is a standing witness — not a broken one.

lessons.heading: Horn one: if the Bible stands, the Quran falls
lessons.body: We can check what the Bible said in Muhammad's day, because our copies are older than Islam: the Dead Sea Scrolls predate Christ, and Codex Sinaiticus (about AD 350) gives us the whole New Testament more than two centuries before Muhammad (AD 570-632). That Bible proclaims the crucifixion and Jesus as the Son of God; the Quran denies both (Q 4:157; 5:72). If the Bible the Quran praised is this Bible, then on the contested points the Quran fails by the witness it chose.

lessons.heading: Horn two: 'it was corrupted' — when?
lessons.body: The usual answer is tahrif: the text was corrupted. Press one question: when? If before Muhammad, the Quran praised a corrupted book and called God's words unchangeable. If after Muhammad, the manuscripts answer: copies older than his lifetime already read as ours do. St. John of Damascus, the first Christian writer to answer Islam (he died about AD 749), already treated it as a splinter off Christianity — this conversation is nearly as old as Islam itself. Keep the aim narrow: we are testing a book's own claims, not attacking the person in front of us.

questions.prompt: What does the Quran tell Christians to judge by?
choices: Their own church traditions
The Gospel in their hands (Q 5:47)
Only the Quran
questions.explanation: Q 5:47: 'Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed therein.' The Quran sends Christians back to their Gospel as a living standard.

questions.prompt: A friend says the Bible was corrupted (tahrif). What is the cleanest first question?
choices: 'Which church do you attend?'
'Why do you pray five times a day?'
'Corrupted when — before or after Muhammad?'
questions.explanation: Timing is the dilemma. 'Before Muhammad' clashes with the Quran praising the earlier Scripture and calling God's words unchangeable (Q 6:115). 'After Muhammad' collides with the manuscript record.

questions.prompt: Why do Codex Sinaiticus and the Dead Sea Scrolls matter in this argument?
choices: They are the first two churches
They prove the biblical text existed centuries before Islam, matching what we read now
They were written by Muhammad's followers
questions.explanation: Sinaiticus (about AD 350) and the Scrolls (before Christ) predate Islam by centuries, so the Bible of Muhammad's day is checkable — and it proclaims the crucifixion and the Son.

lessonsEs.heading: El planteo: el Corán señala hacia la Biblia
lessonsEs.body: El Corán llama a la Torá y al Evangelio libros revelados por Dios. Les dice a los judíos que juzguen por la Torá y a los cristianos por el Evangelio (Corán 5:43-47), le dice a Mahoma, si está en duda, que pregunte a quienes leían la Escritura antes que él (Corán 10:94), e insiste en que nadie puede cambiar las palabras de Dios (Corán 6:115; 18:27). En sus propios términos, entonces, la Biblia es un testigo que sigue en pie, no uno roto.

En sus propios términos, entonces, la Biblia es un testigo que sigue en pie, no uno roto.

lessonsEs.heading: El primer cuerno: si la Biblia se sostiene, el Corán cae
lessonsEs.body: Podemos comprobar qué decía la Biblia en los días de Mahoma, porque nuestras copias son más antiguas que el islam: los Rollos del Mar Muerto son anteriores a Cristo, y el Códice Sinaítico (hacia el año 350) nos da todo el Nuevo Testamento más de dos siglos antes de Mahoma (570-632). Esa Biblia proclama la crucifixión y a Jesús como Hijo de Dios; el Corán niega las dos cosas (Corán 4:157; 5:72). Si la Biblia que el Corán alabó es esta Biblia, entonces en los puntos en disputa el Corán falla por el testigo que él mismo eligió.

lessonsEs.bodyEs: Podemos comprobar qué decía la Biblia en los días de Mahoma, porque nuestras copias son más antiguas que el islam: los Rollos del Mar Muerto son anteriores a Cristo, y el Códice Sinaítico (hacia el año 350) nos da todo el Nuevo Testamento más de dos siglos antes de Mahoma (570-632). Esa Biblia proclama la crucifixión y a Jesús como Hijo de Dios; el Corán niega las dos cosas (Corán 4:157; 5:72). Si la Biblia que el Corán alabó es esta Biblia, entonces en los puntos en disputa el Corán falla por el testigo que él mismo eligió.

lessonsEs.heading: El segundo cuerno: “se corrompió”: ¿cuándo?
lessonsEs.body: La respuesta habitual es el tahrif: el texto se corrompió. Aprieta una sola pregunta: ¿cuándo? Si fue antes de Mahoma, el Corán alabó un libro corrompido y llamó inmutables las palabras de Dios. Si fue después de Mahoma, los manuscritos responden: copias más antiguas que su vida ya se leen como las nuestras. San Juan Damasceno, el primer escritor cristiano que respondió al islam (murió hacia el año 749), ya lo trataba como una astilla desprendida del cristianismo: esta conversación es casi tan antigua como el islam mismo. Mantén estrecho el objetivo: estamos probando las afirmaciones propias de un libro, no atacando a la persona que tienes delante.

challenges.title: Genesis: beginnings and promise
challenges.level: 6 teaching cards · 9 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Creation, the human image, and Abraham’s promise. God created from overflowing goodness, not from need.
challenges.source: Genesis 1–3; 12:1–3

lessons.heading: The book
lessons.body: Orthodox reading receives Genesis as the beginning of creation and God’s covenant story. The same God who creates also seeks humanity after the fall.

lessons.heading: The image
lessons.body: St Athanasius reads humanity made in God’s image in light of the Word who comes to renew that image. See Genesis 1:26–27 and John 1:14.

lessons.heading: The promise
lessons.body: God calls Abraham and promises blessing to the families of the earth. Paul connects that promise with the Gospel in Galatians 3:8.

lessons.heading: God the Creator
lessons.body: God’s love was already perfect inside the Trinity, so creation was not a need. In the communion of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, each Person is already lover and beloved. Nothing was missing, and nothing outside God could complete Him. Creation is the overflow of a goodness that, by its nature, wants to be shared. St John of Damascus puts it this way: the good God was not content to contemplate Himself, but by a superabundance of goodness willed that others should benefit from that goodness and share it, and so He brings all things from nothing into being. Say it in your own words before you go on: God did not create because He was lonely or incomplete. He created because perfect love overflows. The world is that sharing, called out of nothing — not a repair of God, and not a craftsman shaping matter that was already there.

lessons.heading: The universe
lessons.body: The six days of Genesis are not six ordinary sunsets. They are successive stages in which the visible world is called out of non-being. That world will not be thrown away at the end. It will not slide back into nothing. It is destined to be taken up into a higher mode of being. And it is not abandoned now. The Holy Spirit broods over the material world as a mother bird over the waters, breathing the spirit of life into it. Matter is loved. It is not a mistake.

lessons.heading: The six days of creation
lessons.body: “Let there be light” is not the creation of the sun. Sun and moon come on the fourth day. The light of the first day is the light of God reflected in what He has made. The days then unfold: heaven and the waters, dry land and plants, the lights of the sky, the living creatures of sea and air, and on the sixth day the animals and humanity. St Anthony, asked how he could live without books, answered that the created world itself was his book. Read Genesis as the Church’s story of a good world brought into being by God’s word, and read the world as that story still speaking.

questions.prompt: What does Genesis say God saw after creating?
choices: That it was good
That it was finished by Adam
That it was hidden
questions.explanation: Genesis repeatedly says God saw that creation was good.

questions.prompt: Where does Genesis say humanity is made in God’s image?
choices: Genesis 1:26–27
Genesis 12:3
Genesis 50:20
questions.explanation: Genesis 1:26–27 says humanity is made in God’s image.

questions.prompt: Who receives the promise of blessing for all families of the earth?
choices: Abraham
Pharaoh
Goliath
questions.explanation: Abraham receives the promise that all families of the earth will be blessed in him.

questions.prompt: Say it back: why was creation not something God needed?
choices: His love was already perfect inside the Trinity, so nothing was missing; creation is goodness overflowing to be shared
He was lonely and incomplete until the world existed
The angels required Him to make a world
questions.explanation: Love was already perfect among Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, each lover and beloved. Creation was not a need. It was the overflow of a goodness that wants to be shared.

questions.prompt: How does St John of Damascus say it?
choices: The good God was not content to contemplate Himself, but willed others to share His goodness
God created because He was dissatisfied with His own life
God became a creature in order to know Himself
questions.explanation: Damascus: the good God was not content to contemplate Himself. By a superabundance of goodness He brings things from nothing so they may share that goodness.

questions.prompt: How should the six days be heard in this reading?
choices: As six ordinary twenty-four-hour days and nothing more
As successive stages by which God calls the visible world out of non-being
As a myth meaning God did not create
questions.explanation: The days are stages of creation, not a denial of creation and not merely six ordinary evenings.

questions.prompt: What happens to the universe at the end, in this reading?
choices: It returns to non-being
It is taken up into a higher mode of being rather than discarded
It replaces God
questions.explanation: What God called out of nothing is not thrown back into nothing. It is destined for a higher mode of being.

questions.prompt: What is the light of the first day?
choices: Sunlight, which is created on the first day
The light of God reflected in created being, before sun and moon
Only a metaphor for human reason
questions.explanation: Sun and moon appear on the fourth day. The first light is God’s light reflected in creation.

questions.prompt: What did St Anthony call his book in the desert?
choices: The created world itself
A library he kept hidden
Only the Psalms, never creation
questions.explanation: Anthony’s answer is that creation itself consoles and teaches. The world is a book.

lessonsEs.body: La lectura ortodoxa recibe Génesis como el comienzo de la creación y de la historia del pacto de Dios. El mismo Dios que crea también busca a la humanidad después de la caída.

lessonsEs.heading: Dios el Creador
lessonsEs.body: El amor de Dios ya era perfecto dentro de la Trinidad, así que la creación no era una necesidad. En la comunión del Padre, del Hijo y del Espíritu Santo, cada Persona ya es amante y amado. No faltaba nada, y nada fuera de Dios podía completarlo. La creación es el desborde de una bondad que, por su naturaleza, quiere compartirse. San Juan Damasceno lo dice así: el Dios bueno no se contentó con contemplarse a sí mismo, sino que, por una sobreabundancia de bondad, quiso que otros se beneficiaran de esa bondad y la compartieran, y así trae todas las cosas de la nada al ser. Dilo con tus propias palabras antes de seguir: Dios no creó porque estuviera solo o incompleto. Creó porque el amor perfecto se desborda. El mundo es ese compartir, llamado de la nada: no un arreglo de Dios, y no un artesano que da forma a una materia que ya estaba ahí.

lessonsEs.heading: El universo
lessonsEs.body: Los seis días de Génesis no son seis atardeceres ordinarios. Son etapas sucesivas en las que el mundo visible es llamado desde el no ser. Ese mundo no se va a desechar al final. No va a resbalar de vuelta a la nada. Está destinado a ser elevado a un modo más alto de ser. Y ahora no está abandonado. El Espíritu Santo se cierne sobre el mundo material como un ave madre sobre las aguas, soplando en él el espíritu de vida. La materia es amada. No es un error.

lessonsEs.heading: Los seis días de la creación
lessonsEs.body: “Sea la luz” no es la creación del sol. El sol y la luna llegan el cuarto día. La luz del primer día es la luz de Dios reflejada en lo que él ha hecho. Luego los días se despliegan: el cielo y las aguas, la tierra seca y las plantas, las lumbreras del cielo, los seres vivos del mar y del aire, y en el sexto día los animales y la humanidad. San Antonio, cuando le preguntaron cómo podía vivir sin libros, respondió que el mundo creado mismo era su libro. Lee Génesis como el relato de la Iglesia de un mundo bueno traído al ser por la palabra de Dios, y lee el mundo como ese relato que todavía habla.

challenges.title: The Gospels: Christ’s life and Pascha
challenges.summary: Four witnesses, incarnation, and resurrection.
challenges.source: John 1; Luke 24

lessons.heading: Four Gospels
lessons.body: Orthodox reading receives Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John as four witnesses to one Lord. Each tells the good news of Jesus Christ.

lessons.heading: The Word made flesh
lessons.body: St Athanasius stresses that the eternal Word truly took our humanity. John 1:14 speaks of the incarnation, not an appearance or disguise.

lessons.heading: Pascha
lessons.body: The risen Christ meets Mary Magdalene and the disciples. Luke 24 and John 20 narrate encounters, not merely a remembered idea.

lessons.heading: Jesus Christ, the New Adam
lessons.body: The first Adam was called to grow into likeness with God and to bring the visible world to God with him. He did not. After the commandment was broken, the way back was closed from our side. Christ takes up the vocation Adam dropped. He is the New Adam: the one human who does not turn the gift back into self-love, and who carries our nature where Adam could not take it. Read the Gospels as that repair from inside the race, not as the story of a teacher who left our nature where He found it.

questions.explanation: Adam was called to deification and to offer the world to God. He did not complete that calling.

questions.explanation: The New Adam carries the human vocation Adam broke, from within the human race.

lessonsEs.heading: Cuatro Evangelios
lessonsEs.body: La lectura ortodoxa recibe a Mateo, Marcos, Lucas y Juan como cuatro testigos de un solo Señor. Cada uno cuenta la buena noticia de Jesucristo.

lessonsEs.heading: El Verbo hecho carne

lessonsEs.heading: Jesucristo, el nuevo Adán
lessonsEs.body: El primer Adán fue llamado a crecer en semejanza con Dios y a llevar con él el mundo visible hacia Dios. No lo hizo. Después de que se rompió el mandamiento, el camino de vuelta quedó cerrado de nuestro lado. Cristo toma la vocación que Adán dejó caer. Es el nuevo Adán: el único humano que no vuelve el don en amor a sí mismo, y que lleva nuestra naturaleza adonde Adán no pudo llevarla. Lee los Evangelios como esa reparación desde dentro de la raza, no como la historia de un maestro que dejó nuestra naturaleza donde la encontró.

lessons.heading: The question

challenges.title: Chalcedon · 451

challenges.source: OCA · Fifth Century, Fourth Ecumenical Council

lessons.heading: One Lord
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching confesses one Jesus Christ, fully divine and fully human, without dividing him into two persons or confusing his natures.

lessons.heading: The Gospel
lessons.body: John 1:14 speaks of the Word becoming flesh; Philippians 2:6–8 speaks of the Son taking the form of a servant.

lessons.heading: The Fathers
lessons.body: St Cyril’s emphasis on the one incarnate Son and the Fathers’ insistence on real humanity both shape careful reading of Chalcedon.

lessons.heading: The unity of natures
lessons.body: Eutyches said that before the union there were two natures, and after it only one. Dioscorus backed him. Chalcedon answered in 451: one hypostasis of God the Word in two natures, divine and human. Each nature keeps its own fullness. Christ is not split into two persons. The definition says it with four fences — without confusion, without change, without division, without separation — because the Fathers were trying to speak the inexpressible without breaking it. “One nature after the union,” if it means the humanity disappeared into the divinity, is the error Chalcedon closed.

lessonsEs.heading: La unidad de las naturalezas
lessonsEs.body: Eutiques dijo que antes de la unión había dos naturalezas, y después solo una. Dióscoro lo respaldó. challenges.title: Constantinople III · 680–681
challenges.summary: Christ has divine and human natural wills.
challenges.source: OCA · Seventh Century, Maximus the Confessor

lessons.heading: Complete humanity
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching confesses that Christ’s full humanity includes a human will. His human willing freely follows the divine will, never opposing it in sin.

lessons.heading: The prayer
lessons.body: In Matthew 26:39, Christ prays in Gethsemane, “not as I will, but as thou wilt.” Read his human obedience without splitting him into two persons.

lessons.heading: The Father
lessons.body: St Maximus the Confessor defended the two natural wills and activities of the one Christ before the Sixth Council.

lessons.heading: Two actions and two wills
lessons.body: Some, while still saying “two natures,” spoke of one divine-human action. That is Monoenergism. Monothelitism went on to say Christ had only a divine will, the human will swallowed up. The hope was a compromise with the Monophysites. St Maximus refused it. Christ, God by nature, wills with the divine will He shares with the Father; Christ, man by nature, wills with a human will that does not fight the Father. Gethsemane is the proof in the Gospel: “not as I will, but as Thou wilt” is a real human will consenting, not a will that has already vanished. Constantinople III (680–681) followed Maximus: two natural wills and two natural energies, without confusion. Maximus paid with his tongue and his hand. The Church kept his confession.

lessonsEs.heading: Dos acciones y dos voluntades
lessonsEs.body: Algunos, aun diciendo “dos naturalezas”, hablaban de una sola acción divino-humana. Eso es el monoenergismo. El monotelismo siguió diciendo que Cristo tenía solo una voluntad divina, y que la voluntad humana quedaba tragada. La esperanza era un compromiso con los monofisitas. San Máximo se negó. Cristo, Dios por naturaleza, quiere con la voluntad divina que comparte con el Padre; Cristo, hombre por naturaleza, quiere con una voluntad humana que no pelea con el Padre. Getsemaní es la prueba en el Evangelio: “no como yo quiero, sino como tú” es una voluntad humana real que consiente, no una voluntad que ya se desvaneció. Constantinopla III (680–681) siguió a Máximo: dos voluntades naturales y dos energías naturales, sin confusión. Máximo pagó con la lengua y con la mano. La Iglesia guardó su confesión.
