challenges.title: Monasticism
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Tonsure is treated as a mystery: a death like baptism, a return toward Paradise, and one path among others to salvation.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: Monasticism
lessons.body: The Orthodox rite of monastic tonsure has a sacramental character. Dionysius and the rite itself call it a mystery. Like baptism, it is a death to a merely fleshly life and a new beginning. Its aim is the chastity and wholeness Adam and Eve had before the Fall — “a life according to the Gospel,” the Fathers said, and “a true philosophy.” The Lord’s own words are its rule: sell what you have, deny yourself, take up the cross, love Him more than father and mother. A monk is the merchant who sells everything for the one pearl. Monasticism was in the Church early and came to the fore in the fourth century, when martyrdom was no longer the ordinary threat and the empire made peace with the faith. The desert became a way to die to the world without waiting for a persecutor. It is one path, as marriage and priesthood are paths. Walked to the end, it leads to salvation and deification. It is not a higher caste of Christians, and it is not an escape from love.

questions.prompt: How is monastic tonsure described?
choices: As a mystery, a death to fleshly life like baptism
As a hobby with no rite
As a denial that marriage can save anyone
questions.explanation: The rite and Dionysius call tonsure a sacrament. It is a death and a beginning, akin to baptism.

questions.prompt: What Gospel words carry the philosophy of monasticism?
choices: Sell what you have, deny yourself, take up the cross, and follow
Build bigger barns
Avoid the poor
questions.explanation: Matthew 19:21, 16:24, and 10:37 are the rule: perfection as following Christ at the cost of everything else.

questions.prompt: What is monasticism among the ways of salvation?
choices: One way, beside marriage and priesthood, if it is walked to the end
The only way
A way that cannot lead to deification
questions.explanation: It is a path, not the only path. Faithfulness to the end is what makes the path saving.

lessonsEs.heading: El monacato
lessonsEs.body: El rito ortodoxo de la tonsura monástica tiene carácter sacramental. Dionisio y el rito mismo lo llaman misterio. Como el bautismo, es una muerte a la vida meramente carnal y un comienzo nuevo. Su meta es la castidad y la integridad que tenían Adán y Eva antes de la caída: “una vida según el Evangelio”, decían los Padres, y “una verdadera filosofía”. Las palabras del Señor son su regla: vende lo que tienes, niégate a ti mismo, toma la cruz, ámalo más que al padre y a la madre. Un monje es el mercader que vende todo por la perla única. El monacato estuvo en la Iglesia desde temprano y pasó al primer plano en el siglo IV, cuando el martirio ya no era la amenaza ordinaria y el imperio hizo las paces con la fe. El desierto se volvió un modo de morir al mundo sin esperar a un perseguidor. Es un camino, como el matrimonio y el sacerdocio son caminos. Recorrido hasta el final, lleva a la salvación y a la deificación. No es una casta superior de cristianos, ni una fuga del amor.

challenges.title: The end of history
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: The Church has always expected Christ’s return. The end is His victory over death, not only a catastrophe to fear.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: The end of history
lessons.body: From the first days the Church has waited for the Lord to come again, because He promised it. That hope is not a hobby for the anxious. It is how Christians read history: it is going somewhere, and the somewhere is a Person. The end is often pictured only as fear — catastrophe, devastation, a world burned down. The catechism will not leave it there. Paul gives the other face: the perishable puts on the imperishable, the mortal puts on immortality, and the saying comes true, “Death is swallowed up in victory.” Expectation of the Second Coming should make a person watchful and merciful, not fascinated by wreckage. The last word is Christ’s, and the last word is life.

questions.prompt: Why has the Church expected the Second Coming from the beginning?
choices: Because the Lord Himself promised He would come again
Because the apostles invented an ending to replace the Cross
Because history has no direction
questions.explanation: The hope rests on Christ’s promise, not on a taste for disaster.

questions.prompt: What does this reading refuse to make the eschaton?
choices: Only a realm of fear and catastrophe
The victory in which death is swallowed up
A reason to stay watchful
questions.explanation: Fear of wreckage is not the whole hope. Paul ends on victory: the mortal puts on immortality.

questions.prompt: Which line is the hope Paul names?
choices: Death is swallowed up in victory
Death is the last god
No one will be raised
questions.explanation: 1 Corinthians 15: the perishable puts on the imperishable. That is the Christian end of history.

challenges.summaryEs: Jesús dice que volverá. La esperanza mira hacia ese día, no hacia una huida.

lessonsEs.heading: El fin de la historia
lessonsEs.body: Desde los primeros días la Iglesia ha esperado que el Señor vuelva, porque Él lo prometió. Esa esperanza no es un pasatiempo para los ansiosos. Es el modo en que los cristianos leen la historia: va hacia algún lugar, y ese lugar es una Persona. El fin suele pintarse solo como miedo: catástrofe, devastación, un mundo quemado. El catecismo no lo deja ahí. Pablo muestra la otra cara: “es menester que esto corruptible sea vestido de incorrupción, y esto mortal sea vestido de inmortalidad”, y entonces se cumple la palabra: “Sorbida es la muerte con victoria” (1 Corintios 15:53–54, RV1909). La espera de la segunda venida debe volverte vigilante y misericordioso, no fascinado por los escombros. La última palabra es de Cristo, y la última palabra es vida.

challenges.title: Death and resurrection
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Death is a mystery and a birth into eternity. The soul waits the Judgment, and mercy remains possible before that day.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: Death and resurrection
lessons.body: St Ignatius Brianchaninov calls death a great mystery: the birth of a person out of passing life into eternity. Christianity does not treat death as the end. Earthly life is preparation for what death opens. The soul does not go out like a candle. The righteous are carried by the angels to the threshold of Paradise, Abraham’s bosom, and they wait there for the Last Judgment. The reading is sober about hell as well: before the Judgment, release is still possible; after it, that possibility closes. Death is serious, and it is not yet the final sentence. Pray for the dead because the story is not finished when the body is buried.

questions.prompt: How does St Ignatius Brianchaninov name death?
choices: A birth from passing life into eternity
The extinction of the person
A punishment with no mystery
questions.explanation: Death is a great mystery and a birth. Earthly life prepares for it; it does not merely stop.

questions.prompt: Where do righteous souls wait, in this reading?
choices: At the threshold of Paradise, called Abraham’s bosom, until the Judgment
Nowhere; they are already judged and gone
In their graves with no soul remaining
questions.explanation: The angels bring them to Abraham’s bosom. They wait for the Last Judgment. They are not annihilated.

questions.prompt: When does the possibility of release from hell come to an end?
choices: After the Last Judgment
At the moment of baptism
It never existed
questions.explanation: Before the Judgment, release remains possible. After it, the reading says that possibility closes. That is why the Church prays for the departed now.

challenges.summaryEs: La muerte es real. La resurrección también, y es del cuerpo, no solo de una idea.

lessonsEs.heading: La muerte y la resurrección
lessonsEs.body: San Ignacio Briancháninov llama a la muerte un gran misterio: el nacimiento de una persona desde la vida que pasa hacia la eternidad. El cristianismo no trata la muerte como el final. La vida terrenal es preparación para lo que la muerte abre. El alma no se apaga como una vela. A los justos los llevan los ángeles hasta el umbral del Paraíso, el seno de Abraham, y allí esperan el Juicio Final. La lectura es sobria también respecto al infierno: antes del Juicio, la liberación todavía es posible; después, esa posibilidad se cierra. La muerte es seria, y todavía no es la sentencia final. Ora por los difuntos, porque la historia no termina cuando el cuerpo es sepultado.

challenges.title: The Last Judgment
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: At death the soul keeps memory and responsibility. Christ’s preaching to the dead means every person is brought to a real choice.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: The Last Judgment
lessons.body: At death the soul leaves the body and does not lose memory, thought, or feeling. It enters the other world carrying the weight of its life. Judgment is not a surprise quiz about forgotten facts. It is the truth of a life, told in the presence of God. The reading lingers on Christ’s descent to the dead. Peter says He preached to those who died in the flood, the righteous for the unrighteous. The point drawn here is astonishing and moral at once: Christ preached in hell so that every person He made might choose good or evil and, with that choice, be saved or condemned. No one is discarded unaddressed. The Judgment honors freedom. It does not sneak up on a soul that was never asked.

questions.prompt: What does the soul carry out of this life?
choices: Memory, thought, feeling, and accountability for its sins
Nothing; personality ends
Only its best public reputation
questions.explanation: Death changes the mode of existence. It does not wipe memory or responsibility.

questions.prompt: Why does this reading say Christ preached in hell?
choices: So that every person might make a real choice for good or evil
To cancel human freedom
Because the Cross had failed
questions.explanation: The descent is preached as Christ’s refusal to leave anyone unaddressed. The choice remains real, and so does the consequence.

questions.prompt: Which text is used for the preaching to the dead?
choices: 1 Peter: Christ preached to those who perished in the flood
A claim that Peter denied the descent
Only a medieval poem
questions.explanation: 1 Peter 3 is the text. Christ, the righteous one, died for the unrighteous and preached to the dead.

lessonsEs.heading: El Juicio Final
lessonsEs.body: En la muerte el alma deja el cuerpo y no pierde la memoria, el pensamiento ni el sentimiento. Entra en el otro mundo cargando el peso de su vida. El juicio no es un examen sorpresa sobre datos olvidados. Es la verdad de una vida, dicha en la presencia de Dios. La lectura se detiene en el descenso de Cristo a los muertos. Pedro dice que predicó a los que murieron en el diluvio, el justo por los injustos: “Porque también Cristo padeció una vez por los pecados, el justo por los injustos, para llevarnos á Dios”, y “también fué y predicó á los espíritus encarcelados”, los desobedientes “en los días de Noé” (1 Pedro 3:18–20, RV1909). El punto que se saca aquí es asombroso y moral a la vez: Cristo predicó en el infierno para que cada persona que Él hizo pudiera elegir el bien o el mal y, con esa elección, ser salvada o condenada. A nadie se lo descarta sin que se le hable. El Juicio honra la libertad. No se le echa encima a un alma a la que nunca se le preguntó.

challenges.title: What is hell?
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Hell is the suffering of a soul that can no longer love. Christ descends into it, and the pedagogy of fear is not the Gospel’s picture.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: What is hell?
lessons.body: Dostoyevsky’s Elder Zosima asks, “What is hell?” and answers: suffering because one can no longer love. That is the image this catechism trusts more than Dante’s catalogue of torments or a medieval pedagogy of fear, with its stress on satisfaction and punishment. Sophrony says he does not see Christ as Michelangelo painted Him, hurling people into the abyss. He sees Christ immensely powerful with the power of unassuming love — and if God is love, He is love even while He judges. Hell is bound to Holy Week and Pascha: Christ descends into the abyss, as He descended into the Jordan, and hell cannot bear His light. It surrenders its prisoners. Hell is real. It is also already sentenced to death. Fear is a poor teacher beside that invasion of love.

questions.prompt: How does Zosima answer “What is hell?”
choices: Suffering because one can no longer love
A dungeon God enjoys
A symbol that nothing is wrong
questions.explanation: The catechism takes hell with full seriousness and names it as the ruin of love, not as a spectacle of cruelty.

questions.prompt: What picture of Christ does Sophrony refuse?
choices: Christ hurling His enemies into the abyss as raw force
Christ powerful in unassuming love, even in judgment
Christ descending to the dead
questions.explanation: Judgment is real, and it is the judgment of love. Michelangelo’s furious Christ is not the revelation Sophrony trusts.

questions.prompt: What does Christ’s descent do to hell?
choices: He illumines it and breaks its hold; hell is sentenced to death
He makes peace with the devil as an equal
He discovers hell is stronger than He is
questions.explanation: As the Jordan was sanctified by His entering it, hell is invaded by His light and cannot keep its prisoners. Hell remains real, and it does not have the last word.

lessonsEs.heading: ¿Qué es el infierno?
lessonsEs.body: El anciano Zósima, de Dostoievski, pregunta: “¿Qué es el infierno?” y responde: el sufrimiento de ya no poder amar. Esa es la imagen en la que este catecismo confía más que en el catálogo de tormentos de Dante o en una pedagogía medieval del miedo, con su peso en la satisfacción y el castigo. Sofronio dice que no ve a Cristo como lo pintó Miguel Ángel, arrojando gente al abismo. Lo ve inmensamente poderoso con el poder de un amor sin ostentación: y si Dios es amor, es amor incluso mientras juzga. El infierno está atado a la Semana Santa y a la Pascua: Cristo desciende al abismo, como descendió al Jordán, y el infierno no puede soportar su luz. Entrega a sus presos. El infierno es real. También está ya condenado a muerte. El miedo es un mal maestro junto a esa invasión del amor.

challenges.title: A new heaven and a new earth
challenges.level: 1 teaching card · 3 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Paradise is a state of the soul in the abundance of love and light. Union with Christ is that life, and not all share it in the same measure.
challenges.source: The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev
challenges.adaptation: Adapted from The Mystery of Faith by Bishop Hilarion Alfeyev.

lessons.heading: A new heaven and a new earth
lessons.body: Paradise is not first a place on a map. It is a condition of the soul. As hell is the suffering of being unable to love, Paradise is the bliss of love and light in abundance. The person united to Christ shares that life wholly. The Father’s house has many rooms: some will rest in a higher measure and some in a lower one, and the difference is not God’s stinginess but the capacity love has grown. The promise of a new heaven and a new earth is the promise that creation itself is not discarded. It is renewed around the people who have become able to live in love. Hope is concrete. It is Christ, shared without end.

questions.prompt: What is Paradise in this reading?
choices: A state of the soul: bliss from the abundance of love and light
Only a location with no change in the person
The same thing as hell
questions.explanation: Paradise answers hell. One is the inability to love; the other is love and light without lack.

questions.prompt: Why are there many rooms in the Father’s house?
choices: People share Christ’s life in different measures, according to the capacity love has grown
God plays favorites with no reason
Most rooms are empty because almost no one is saved
questions.explanation: The difference is real and it is not cruelty. Union with Christ is full for the person who is united to Him, and measures still differ.

questions.prompt: What happens to creation in this hope?
choices: It is renewed, not thrown away
It is abandoned as a mistake
It replaces Christ
questions.explanation: A new heaven and a new earth means the world God made is transfigured around those who can live in love.

challenges.titleEs: Un cielo nuevo y una tierra nueva
challenges.summaryEs: El final no es escapar del mundo. Es el mundo hecho nuevo.

lessonsEs.heading: Un cielo nuevo y una tierra nueva
lessonsEs.body: El Paraíso no es primero un lugar en un mapa. Es una condición del alma. Así como el infierno es el sufrimiento de no poder amar, el Paraíso es la dicha del amor y de la luz en abundancia. La persona unida a Cristo comparte esa vida por entero. “En la casa de mi Padre muchas moradas hay” (Juan 14:2, RV1909): algunos descansarán en una medida más alta y otros en una más baja, y la diferencia no es la mezquindad de Dios, sino la capacidad que el amor ha hecho crecer. La promesa de un cielo nuevo y una tierra nueva es la promesa de que la creación misma no se descarta. Se renueva alrededor de las personas que se han vuelto capaces de vivir en el amor. La esperanza es concreta. Es Cristo, compartido sin fin.

challenges.title: Mary, the Theotokos
challenges.summary: The Church calls Mary Theotokos because the one she bore is the Son of God.
challenges.source: Luke 1 and John 19 in the King James text; the title Theotokos was confessed at the Council of Ephesus (431). The hymn line is from Isabel Florence Hapgood, Service Book (Houghton, Mifflin, 1906), public domain.

lessons.heading: The mother of the Lord
lessons.body:
Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, asks Mary, “And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). The Church kept that name. Mary is not the source of the Godhead. She is the woman from whom the eternal Son took flesh. At Ephesus in 431 the Church called her Theotokos, the Birth-giver of God, so that no one would split the child into a mere man standing beside the Word.

From the cross Jesus gives her to the beloved disciple: “Woman, behold thy son,” and to the disciple, “Behold thy mother” (John 19:26–27). The Church still stands with her. A public-domain hymn of the hours says, “More honourable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim, thou who without defilement barest God the Word, true Birth-giver of God, we magnify thee.”

lessons.heading: How to speak of her
lessons.body: Honor Mary without turning her into a goddess, and do not shrink her into an ordinary mother of an ordinary prophet. She said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word” (Luke 1:38). That yes is the pattern of the Church: a creature who receives God and does not replace him.

questions.prompt: Why does the Church call Mary Theotokos?
choices: Because she is the source of the Father
Because the one she bore is the Son of God in the flesh
Because she wrote the Gospels
questions.explanation: Theotokos guards the identity of the child: Mary bore the incarnate Son, not a second person beside the Word.

questions.prompt: In Luke 1:43, Elizabeth calls Mary the mother of whom?
choices: My Lord
A prophet only
The emperor
questions.explanation: Elizabeth says, “the mother of my Lord.”

lessonsEs.heading: La madre del Señor
lessonsEs.body:
Isabel, llena del Espíritu Santo, le pregunta a María: “¿Y de dónde esto á mí, que la madre de mi Señor venga á mí?” (Lucas 1:43, RV1909). La Iglesia guardó ese nombre. María no es la fuente de la divinidad. Es la mujer de quien el Hijo eterno tomó carne. En Éfeso, en el año 431, la Iglesia la llamó Theotokos, la que dio a luz a Dios, para que nadie partiera al niño en un simple hombre puesto al lado del Verbo.

Desde la cruz Jesús se la entrega al discípulo amado: “Mujer, he ahí tu hijo”, y al discípulo: “He ahí tu madre” (Juan 19:26–27, RV1909). La Iglesia sigue de pie con ella. Un himno de las horas, de dominio público, dice: “Más honorable que los querubines e incomparablemente más gloriosa que los serafines, tú que sin corrupción diste a luz a Dios el Verbo, verdadera Madre de Dios, te magnificamos”.

Isabel, llena del Espíritu Santo, le pregunta a María: “¿Y de dónde esto á mí, que la madre de mi Señor venga á mí?” (Lucas 1:43, RV1909). La Iglesia guardó ese nombre. María no es la fuente de la divinidad. Es la mujer de quien el Hijo eterno tomó carne. En Éfeso, en el año 431, la Iglesia la llamó Theotokos, la que dio a luz a Dios, para que nadie partiera al niño en un simple hombre puesto al lado del Verbo.

Desde la cruz Jesús se la entrega al discípulo amado: “Mujer, he ahí tu hijo”, y al discípulo: “He ahí tu madre” (Juan 19:26–27, RV1909). La Iglesia sigue de pie con ella. Un himno de las horas, de dominio público, dice: “Más honorable que los querubines e incomparablemente más gloriosa que los serafines, tú que sin corrupción diste a luz a Dios el Verbo, verdadera Madre de Dios, te magnificamos”.

lessonsEs.heading: Cómo hablar de ella
lessonsEs.body: Honra a María sin convertirla en una diosa, y no la reduzcas a una madre ordinaria de un profeta ordinario. Ella dijo: “He aquí la sierva del Señor; hágase á mí conforme á tu palabra” (Lucas 1:38, RV1909). Ese sí es el modelo de la Iglesia: una criatura que recibe a Dios y no lo reemplaza.

challenges.title: Saint Nicholas of Myra
challenges.summary: The Church remembers Nicholas as a bishop who hid his alms and stood for the faith.
challenges.source: The Church’s memory of Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia, in the age of the Council of Nicaea. This lesson is original prose and does not quote a modern biography.

lessons.heading: A bishop who gave in secret
lessons.body:
Nicholas was a bishop of Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, in the early fourth century. The Church remembers him in the same age as the Council of Nicaea, when the bishops confessed that the Son is of one essence with the Father. What ordinary people remembered first was not a speech. It was that he found a way to give without being seen.

The old stories say he provided dowries for daughters whose father was about to sell them into shame, and that he left the gold where the family would find it and he would not. Whether every detail of those stories can be dated, the shape of them matches the Gospel he preached. Jesus says, “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Matthew 6:3). Nicholas became the icon of that sentence.

lessons.heading: What the Church kept
lessons.body: Later ages piled legends on him, and some of those legends are too late to treat as a court record. The Church did not keep him because he is useful for winter tales. She keeps a bishop who defended the poor and the faith of Nicaea. On his day, the fitting response is alms given quietly, not a performance of generosity.

choices: Myra

questions.explanation: The Church remembers Nicholas as bishop of Myra in Lycia.

questions.prompt: Matthew 6:3 tells the giver to hide the gift even from whom?
choices: The left hand

questions.explanation: Jesus says the left hand should not know what the right hand is doing.

lessonsEs.heading: Un obispo que daba en secreto
lessonsEs.body:
Nicolás fue obispo de Mira, en la costa sur del Asia Menor, a comienzos del siglo IV. La Iglesia lo recuerda en la misma época del Concilio de Nicea, cuando los obispos confesaron que el Hijo es de una sola esencia con el Padre. Lo que la gente sencilla recordó primero no fue un discurso. Fue que encontró el modo de dar sin que lo vieran.

Las historias antiguas dicen que consiguió las dotes de unas hijas cuyo padre estaba a punto de venderlas a la vergüenza, y que dejó el oro donde la familia lo hallaría y él no. Aunque no se pueda fechar cada detalle de esas historias, su forma coincide con el Evangelio que predicaba. Jesús dice: “Mas cuando tú haces limosna, no sepa tu izquierda lo que hace tu derecha” (Mateo 6:3, RV1909). Nicolás se volvió el ícono de esa frase.

challenges.title: Saint Seraphim of Sarov
challenges.summary: A Russian monk who received visitors in peace and died at Sarov in 1833.
challenges.source: Historical outline of Seraphim of Sarov (died 1833). This lesson is original prose. It does not quote later books about him.

lessons.heading: A monk at Sarov
lessons.body:
Seraphim lived as a monk at the monastery of Sarov in Russia and died in 1833. He spent long years in a cell and in the forest, then in his last years received the people who walked out to see him. The Church remembers a man who greeted visitors as if the resurrection had already reached the doorway.

He is not a substitute for the Gospels. He is a witness that the same Spirit who filled the apostles is not locked in the first century. People came with ordinary troubles. He answered with prayer, a short word, and the sign of the cross, and sent them back to confession and the chalice.

lessons.heading: What we do not pretend to quote
lessons.body: Many English books about Seraphim are modern and copyrighted. This lesson does not borrow their sentences. What can be said from the public record is enough: a monk of Sarov, a life of prayer, a death in 1833, and a Church that still asks his prayers. The goal of that memory is not nostalgia. It is to seek the Holy Spirit with the same steadiness.

questions.explanation: Seraphim of Sarov died in 1833.

lessonsEs.heading: Un monje en Sarov
lessonsEs.body:
Serafín vivió como monje en el monasterio de Sarov, en Rusia, y murió en 1833. Pasó largos años en una celda y en el bosque, y en sus últimos años recibió a la gente que caminaba hasta él. La Iglesia recuerda a un hombre que saludaba a los visitantes como si la resurrección ya hubiera llegado a la puerta.

No es un sustituto de los Evangelios. Es un testigo de que el mismo Espíritu que llenó a los apóstoles no está encerrado en el siglo I. La gente llegaba con penas ordinarias. Él respondía con oración, una palabra breve y la señal de la cruz, y los devolvía a la confesión y al cáliz.

challenges.title: Saint Herman of Alaska
challenges.summary: A monk from Valaam who stayed in Alaska and died on Spruce Island in 1837.
challenges.source: Historical outline of Herman of Alaska (died 1837). Original prose; no modern biography is quoted.

lessons.heading: From Valaam to Spruce Island
lessons.body:
Herman was a monk of Valaam, in the north of Russia, who traveled with a small mission to Alaska at the end of the eighteenth century. The others died or returned. He stayed. He lived on Spruce Island, near Kodiak, taught the children, cared for the sick, and defended the native people when traders treated them as cargo. He died in 1837.

His life is a mission story without a garrison. He did not arrive as a governor. He arrived as a monk, and the people who buried him had learned the prayers he kept. The Church in America still begins many of her memories with his name.

lessons.heading: A witness, not a slogan
lessons.body: Herman’s love of the people around him was concrete: food, teaching, and a refusal to look away when the weak were cheated. James says, “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (James 1:27). That verse is a fair measure of the life the Church remembers on Spruce Island.

questions.explanation: James names both mercy to the afflicted and a life kept unspotted.

lessonsEs.heading: De Valaam a la isla Spruce
lessonsEs.body:
Germán fue monje de Valaam, en el norte de Rusia, y viajó con una misión pequeña a Alaska a finales del siglo XVIII. Los demás murieron o regresaron. Él se quedó. Vivió en la isla Spruce, cerca de Kodiak, enseñó a los niños, cuidó a los enfermos y defendió a los pueblos nativos cuando los comerciantes los trataban como carga. Murió en 1837.

Su vida es una historia de misión sin guarnición. No llegó como gobernador. Llegó como monje, y la gente que lo sepultó había aprendido las oraciones que él guardaba. La Iglesia en América todavía empieza muchos de sus recuerdos con su nombre.

Ese versículo es una medida justa de la vida que la Iglesia recuerda en la isla Spruce.

challenges.title: Saint Mary of Egypt
challenges.summary: The Church remembers a woman who left a destructive life and finished it in repentance beyond the Jordan.
challenges.source: The ancient commemoration of Mary of Egypt, told in the Church from the life associated with Sophronius of Jerusalem. This lesson is original prose and does not reproduce a modern translation of that life.

lessons.heading: A life turned around
lessons.body:
The Church keeps the memory of Mary of Egypt in Great Lent, especially on the fifth Sunday and on her day in April. The old account says she lived for years in Alexandria in open sexual sin, then came to Jerusalem with a crowd and could not enter the church of the Resurrection. She prayed before an icon of the Mother of God, promised to repent, and crossed the Jordan into the desert.

Years later a priest named Zosimas met her there. She asked for the Holy Mysteries, received them, and died. The details belong to the Church’s received story of her, not to a modern novel. The point the fast is meant to hear is simple: no past is too twisted for repentance, and repentance is a long obedience, not a mood.

lessons.heading: Why Lent tells her story
lessons.body: Lent is not a contest in looking serious. It is a return. The prodigal says, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15:18). Mary’s story is that sentence lived in the desert. The Church puts it before Holy Week so that no one will think the passion is only for people who have been tidy all year.

choices: In Great Lent

On Pentecost alone
questions.explanation: Her commemoration is kept in Great Lent, including the fifth Sunday.

questions.prompt: In the Church’s story, who brought her the Holy Mysteries?
choices: Zosimas

King Herod
questions.explanation: The received account names the priest Zosimas.

lessonsEs.heading: Una vida que dio la vuelta
lessonsEs.body:
La Iglesia guarda la memoria de María de Egipto en la Gran Cuaresma, sobre todo el quinto domingo y en su día de abril. El relato antiguo dice que vivió años en Alejandría en un pecado sexual abierto, luego llegó a Jerusalén con una multitud y no pudo entrar en la iglesia de la Resurrección. Oró ante un ícono de la Madre de Dios, prometió arrepentirse y cruzó el Jordán hacia el desierto.

Años después un sacerdote llamado Zósimas la encontró allí. Ella pidió los Santos Misterios, los recibió y murió. Los detalles pertenecen a la historia recibida de la Iglesia, no a una novela moderna. El punto que el ayuno quiere que escuches es sencillo: ningún pasado está demasiado torcido para el arrepentimiento, y el arrepentimiento es una obediencia larga, no un estado de ánimo.

La historia de María es esa frase vivida en el desierto. La Iglesia la pone antes de la Semana Santa para que nadie piense que la Pasión es solo para quienes se han portado bien todo el año.

challenges.title: Saint John Chrysostom
challenges.summary: The golden-mouthed archbishop of Constantinople, whose homilies still sit beside the New Testament.
challenges.source: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Romans, Homily 1, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, volume 11.

lessons.heading: A preacher of the text
lessons.body:
John was born in Antioch, preached there for years, and then became archbishop of Constantinople. He was sent into exile and died on the road in 407. The name Chrysostom means golden mouth. It stuck because he opened the Scriptures in church and would not stop until the congregation had heard the passage, not a speech floating free of it.

At the start of his homilies on Romans he notices something small and telling: “Moses having written five books, has nowhere put his own name to them, neither have they who after him put together the history of events after him, no nor yet has Matthew, nor John, nor Mark, nor Luke; but the blessed Paul everywhere in his Epistles sets his own name.” John then asks why. That is his method. He stays with the words.

lessons.heading: Why the Church still reads him
lessons.body: Chrysostom is not infallible in every historical guess, and the English in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers is a nineteenth-century translation of his Greek. What the Church received from him is a habit: read the verse, then the next verse, and let doctrine come out of the reading. His Divine Liturgy is the one most Sundays still pray. The preacher and the prayer belong together.

questions.prompt: In the Romans homily quoted here, who puts his own name on his writings?
choices: Paul, in the Epistles
Moses, on all five books
No biblical writer
questions.explanation: Chrysostom says Moses and the evangelists do not sign their books, but Paul sets his name on the Epistles.

questions.prompt: Chrysostom died in what year?
questions.explanation: John Chrysostom died in exile in 407.

lessonsEs.heading: Un predicador del texto
lessonsEs.body:
Juan nació en Antioquía, predicó allí durante años y después fue arzobispo de Constantinopla. Lo enviaron al exilio y murió en el camino, en el año 407. El nombre Crisóstomo significa boca de oro. Se le quedó porque abría las Escrituras en la iglesia y no paraba hasta que la asamblea hubiera oído el pasaje, no un discurso suelto de él.

Al comienzo de sus homilías sobre Romanos nota algo pequeño y revelador: “Moisés, habiendo escrito cinco libros, en ninguna parte les puso su propio nombre, ni tampoco quienes después de él reunieron la historia de los hechos posteriores, ni Mateo, ni Juan, ni Marcos, ni Lucas; pero el bienaventurado Pablo pone su propio nombre en todas partes en sus epístolas”. Juan entonces pregunta por qué. Ese es su método. Se queda con las palabras.

lessonsEs.heading: Por qué la Iglesia todavía lo lee
lessonsEs.body: Crisóstomo no es infalible en cada conjetura histórica, y el texto de los Padres nicenos y postnicenos es una traducción del siglo XIX de su griego. Lo que la Iglesia recibió de él es un hábito: lee el versículo, luego el siguiente, y deja que la doctrina salga de la lectura. Su Divina Liturgia es la que todavía se reza la mayoría de los domingos. El predicador y la oración van juntos.

Lo que la Iglesia recibió de él es un hábito: lee el versículo, luego el siguiente, y deja que la doctrina salga de la lectura. Su Divina Liturgia es la que todavía se reza la mayoría de los domingos. El predicador y la oración van juntos.

challenges.title: Saint Basil the Great
challenges.summary: Bishop of Caesarea, preacher on Genesis, and a founder of the common monastic life.
challenges.source: Basil the Great, Hexaemeron, Homily 1, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, volume 8.

lessons.heading: Creation has an author
lessons.body:
Basil was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the fourth century, brother of Gregory of Nyssa and friend of Gregory of Nazianzus. He organized communities of monks under a common rule, cared for the poor in a large hostel by the city, and preached through the six days of creation.

Opening those homilies, he refuses a fashionable guess: “I am about to speak of the creation of heaven and earth, which was not spontaneous, as some have imagined, but drew its origin from God.” The world is gift. It did not invent itself. Basil’s point is worship before it is science: if creation has an origin, the origin is God.

lessons.heading: A life that matched the preaching
lessons.body: Basil’s name is also on a Divine Liturgy still used on some days of the year, including the Sundays of Great Lent. The same man who said the world came from God built a place where the sick could lie down. Doctrine and mercy were not two hobbies. They were one bishop’s work.

lessonsEs.heading: La creación tiene un autor
lessonsEs.body:
Basilio fue obispo de Cesarea de Capadocia en el siglo IV, hermano de Gregorio de Nisa y amigo de Gregorio Nacianceno. Organizó comunidades de monjes bajo una regla común, cuidó a los pobres en un gran albergue junto a la ciudad y predicó a lo largo de los seis días de la creación.

Al abrir esas homilías, rechaza una conjetura de moda: “Voy a hablar de la creación del cielo y de la tierra, que no fue espontánea, como algunos imaginaron, sino que tuvo su origen en Dios”. El mundo es don. No se inventó solo. El punto de Basilio es adoración antes que ciencia: si la creación tiene un origen, el origen es Dios.

challenges.title: Saint Paisios of Mount Athos
challenges.summary: A monk of Athos who died in 1994, remembered for plain counsel and mercy.
challenges.source: Public facts of Paisios of Mount Athos (died 1994). Original prose. His books and recorded sayings are not quoted, because those publications are not public-domain texts.

lessons.heading: A recent witness
lessons.body:
Paisios was a monk on Mount Athos, the monastic peninsula in northern Greece. He died in 1994. The Church later added him to the calendar of saints. People came to his cell with fears about family, illness, and the state of the world. He answered as a monk: prayer, fasting, and a word that sent the visitor back to confession rather than to a personality cult.

Because he died so recently, almost every English book of his sayings is still in copyright. This lesson does not repeat those pages. A saint does not need a borrowed quotation to be remembered. He needs the truth of his life: a monk who stayed at his prayers and did not despise the people at the door.

lessons.heading: What to imitate
lessons.body: The useful imitation is not a costume. It is the hidden rule he kept: say the Jesus Prayer, tell the truth kindly, and refuse despair. Paul writes, “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God” (Philippians 4:6). That is an old sentence. It is also the shape of a modern monk’s counsel.

lessonsEs.heading: Un testigo reciente
lessonsEs.body:
Paisios fue monje en el Monte Athos, la península monástica del norte de Grecia. Murió en 1994. La Iglesia lo añadió después al calendario de los santos. La gente llegaba a su celda con miedos sobre la familia, la enfermedad y el estado del mundo. Él respondía como monje: oración, ayuno y una palabra que devolvía al visitante a la confesión, no a un culto a la personalidad.

Como murió hace tan poco, casi todos los libros de sus dichos siguen bajo derechos de autor. Esta lección no repite esas páginas. Un santo no necesita una cita prestada para ser recordado. Necesita la verdad de su vida: un monje que se quedó en sus oraciones y no despreció a la gente de la puerta.

lessonsEs.heading: Qué imitar
lessonsEs.body: La imitación útil no es un disfraz. Es la regla escondida que él guardaba: di la oración de Jesús, di la verdad con bondad y rechaza la desesperación. Pablo escribe: “Por nada estéis afanosos; sino sean notorias vuestras peticiones delante de Dios en toda oración y ruego, con hacimiento de gracias” (Filipenses 4:6, RV1909). Es una frase antigua. También es la forma del consejo de un monje moderno.

challenges.title: A walk through the Divine Liturgy
challenges.summary: The Sunday service moves from the Word to the table, and both belong to one prayer.
challenges.source: Original description of the received shape of the Divine Liturgy. The communion prayer quoted here is from Isabel Florence Hapgood, Service Book (1906), public domain. Modern service books are not quoted.

lessons.heading: From the door to the Gospel
lessons.body:
The Divine Liturgy is the Church’s Sunday thanksgiving. It begins with a blessing and the great litany, the long “Lord, have mercy” in which the living and the dead are named. Antiphons and the hymns of the day follow. At the little entrance the Gospel book is carried out. The Church is saying that Christ comes to speak before he comes to be received.

The Trisagion, the prokeimenon, the Epistle, and the Gospel are not a preface that could be skipped. They are the table set in words. The homily, when it is given, is meant to open that reading, not to replace it. Then the Church prays again for the world and for the catechumens, and the faithful remain for the sacrifice of praise.

lessons.heading: From the gifts to the cup
lessons.body:
At the great entrance the bread and wine are brought to the altar. The Creed is said. The anaphora lifts them with thanksgiving: the priest recalls the Father’s work, the cross, and the resurrection, and calls on the Holy Spirit. The Church sings the Lord’s Prayer and comes to the cup.

Before communion a public-domain prayer says, “I believe, O Lord, and I confess, that thou art in very truth the Christ, the Son of the living God, who didst come into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.” The Liturgy ends with thanksgiving and a dismissal. It is one arc: hear the Word, thank the Father, receive the Son, and go in the Spirit.

lessonsEs.heading: De la puerta al Evangelio
lessonsEs.body:
La Divina Liturgia es la acción de gracias dominical de la Iglesia. Empieza con una bendición y la gran letanía, el largo “Señor, ten piedad” en el que se nombra a los vivos y a los muertos. Siguen las antífonas y los himnos del día. En la pequeña entrada se saca el Evangeliario. La Iglesia está diciendo que Cristo viene a hablar antes de venir a ser recibido.

El Trisagio, el prokímeno, la Epístola y el Evangelio no son un prefacio que se pueda saltar. Son la mesa puesta en palabras. La homilía, cuando se da, está llamada a abrir esa lectura, no a reemplazarla. Después la Iglesia ora otra vez por el mundo y por los catecúmenos, y los fieles permanecen para el sacrificio de alabanza.

lessonsEs.heading: De los dones al cáliz
lessonsEs.body:
En la gran entrada se llevan el pan y el vino al altar. Se dice el Credo. La anáfora los eleva con acción de gracias: el sacerdote recuerda la obra del Padre, la cruz y la resurrección, e invoca al Espíritu Santo. La Iglesia canta el Padrenuestro y se acerca al cáliz.

Antes de la comunión, una oración de dominio público dice: “Creo, Señor, y confieso que tú eres verdaderamente el Cristo, el Hijo de Dios vivo, que viniste al mundo para salvar a los pecadores, de los cuales yo soy el primero”. La Liturgia termina con la acción de gracias y una despedida. Es un solo arco: oír la Palabra, dar gracias al Padre, recibir al Hijo y salir en el Espíritu.

challenges.title: Vespers, in plain steps
challenges.summary: The evening service lights the lamps, sings the psalms, and hands the day back to God.
challenges.source: Original account of the received order of Vespers. The evening line quoted here is from Isabel Florence Hapgood, Service Book (1906), public domain.

lessons.heading: Why the Church prays at lamp-lighting
lessons.body:
Vespers is the Church’s evening prayer. It belongs to the start of the liturgical day, because the old way of counting a day began at sunset. The service opens with a blessing and Psalm 104, the psalm of creation: the God who made light is asked to receive the day that is ending. A litany follows. Then come the evening psalms and the hymns appointed for the feast or the fast.

At the heart of the service the lamps are lit and the ancient hymn at lamp-lighting is sung. The Church does not treat darkness as a mood to decorate. She answers it with praise. After that come the readings when a feast has them, the litanies, and the prayer that the evening may be peaceable.

lessons.heading: A lay way in
lessons.body: You do not have to invent a private vespers if you can get to church. If you are at home, the same shape still helps: thank God for the day, read a psalm, ask mercy, and stop. Hapgood’s evening prayers include the line, “The day is past; I thank thee, O Lord.” That is enough of a door. The point is not to collect offices. The point is to let the day end in front of God instead of in front of a screen.

questions.prompt: Which psalm traditionally opens the Church’s Vespers?

questions.explanation: Vespers begins from Psalm 104, blessing God for the created world as the day ends.

questions.prompt: Why does the liturgical day lean toward evening?
choices: The old counting of a day began at sunset
Because morning prayer was forbidden
Because the Gospels were written at night
questions.explanation: The Church inherited a day that turns at sunset, so Vespers opens what morning will continue.

lessonsEs.heading: Por qué la Iglesia ora al encender las lámparas
lessonsEs.body:
Las Vísperas son la oración de la tarde de la Iglesia. Pertenecen al comienzo del día litúrgico, porque la manera antigua de contar un día empezaba en la puesta del sol. El oficio se abre con una bendición y el Salmo 104, el salmo de la creación: al Dios que hizo la luz se le pide que reciba el día que termina. Sigue una letanía. Luego vienen los salmos de la tarde y los himnos señalados para la fiesta o el ayuno.

En el corazón del oficio se encienden las lámparas y se canta el himno antiguo del lucernario. La Iglesia no trata la oscuridad como un estado de ánimo para decorar. Le responde con alabanza. Después vienen las lecturas cuando una fiesta las tiene, las letanías y la oración de que la tarde sea en paz.

lessonsEs.heading: Una entrada para quien está en casa
lessonsEs.body: No tienes que inventarte unas vísperas privadas si puedes llegar a la iglesia. Si estás en casa, la misma forma sigue ayudando: da gracias a Dios por el día, lee un salmo, pide misericordia y detente. Las oraciones de la tarde de Hapgood incluyen la línea: “El día pasó; te doy gracias, Señor”. Con eso basta para una puerta. El punto no es coleccionar oficios. El punto es dejar que el día termine delante de Dios y no delante de una pantalla.

challenges.title: The Jesus Prayer
challenges.summary: A short prayer built from two Gospel cries: the blind man, and the publican.
challenges.source: Mark 10:47 and Luke 18:13 in the King James text. The lesson does not quote a modern manual of the Jesus Prayer.

lessons.heading: Two sentences the Gospels already pray
lessons.body:
Outside Jericho a blind man cries, “Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me” (Mark 10:47). In the temple a publican will not lift his eyes and says, “God be merciful to me a sinner” (Luke 18:13). The Church put those two cries together and kept them short: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.

The prayer is not a spell. It is a name and a need. You can say it on a rope of knots, or under your breath while you walk, or once, slowly, when you have no other words. The point is attention. The name of Jesus is the content. Mercy is the request. The last words keep the speaker honest.

lessons.heading: A pace that can last
lessons.body: The old counsel is to say it gently and to stay with it, not to hunt for a feeling. If the mind wanders, begin the sentence again. Luke says the publican “went down to his house justified” rather than the man who rehearsed his virtues (Luke 18:14). The Jesus Prayer takes that side of the story. It is a way of standing in the truth without making a speech.

questions.explanation: He cries, “have mercy on me.”

questions.explanation: The publican says, “God be merciful to me a sinner.”

challenges.summaryEs: Una oración corta hecha de dos gritos del Evangelio: el ciego y el publicano.

lessonsEs.heading: Dos frases que los Evangelios ya oran
lessonsEs.body:
A las afueras de Jericó un ciego grita: “Jesús, Hijo de David, ten misericordia de mí” (Marcos 10:47, RV1909). En el templo un publicano ni siquiera quiere alzar los ojos y dice: “Dios, sé propicio á mí pecador” (Lucas 18:13, RV1909). La Iglesia juntó esos dos gritos y los dejó cortos: Señor Jesucristo, Hijo de Dios, ten misericordia de mí, pecador.

La oración no es un conjuro. Es un nombre y una necesidad. Puedes decirla en un cordón de nudos, o en voz baja mientras caminas, o una sola vez, despacio, cuando no te quedan otras palabras. El punto es la atención. El nombre de Jesús es el contenido. La misericordia es el pedido. Las últimas palabras mantienen honesto a quien ora.

El punto es la atención. El nombre de Jesús es el contenido. La misericordia es el pedido. Las últimas palabras mantienen honesto a quien ora.

lessonsEs.heading: Un ritmo que puede durar
lessonsEs.body: El consejo antiguo es decirla con suavidad y quedarte ahí, no salir a cazar un sentimiento. Si la mente se va, empieza la frase otra vez. Lucas dice que el publicano “descendió á su casa justificado” antes que el hombre que repasaba sus virtudes (Lucas 18:14, RV1909). La oración de Jesús se pone de ese lado de la historia. Es una manera de estar en la verdad sin dar un discurso.

challenges.title: The Nativity of the Theotokos
challenges.summary: On September 8 the Church begins the year of feasts with Mary’s birth.
challenges.source: The Church’s calendar of the Twelve Great Feasts. Scripture from the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: A birth that prepares a birth
lessons.body:
The Nativity of the Theotokos is kept on September 8. It is the first of the Twelve Great Feasts. The Gospels do not narrate Mary’s birth. The Church receives the story of Joachim and Anna from her older tradition and celebrates the fact the Gospels assume: the mother of the Lord was born of human parents, in a real family, inside the people of Israel.

The feast is not a distraction from Christ. It is the door of the story that ends at his cradle and his cross. Mary will say yes. Until then, the Church simply gives thanks that the woman who will bear him has come into the world.

lessons.heading: Where it sits in the year
lessons.body: September opens the festal cycle. The Exaltation of the Cross follows on the 14th, then the Entrance of the Theotokos in November, and the Nativity of Christ in December. Learning the twelve feasts is a way of learning the Gospel in the order the Church sings it. This one says: salvation arrives through a daughter of Adam, not around her.

lessonsEs.heading: Un nacimiento que prepara un nacimiento
lessonsEs.body:
La Natividad de la Theotokos se celebra el 8 de septiembre. Es la primera de las Doce Grandes Fiestas. Los Evangelios no narran el nacimiento de María. La Iglesia recibe la historia de Joaquín y Ana de su tradición más antigua y celebra el hecho que los Evangelios dan por sentado: la madre del Señor nació de padres humanos, en una familia de verdad, dentro del pueblo de Israel.

La fiesta no es una distracción de Cristo. Es la puerta de la historia que termina en su cuna y en su cruz. María va a decir que sí. Hasta entonces, la Iglesia simplemente da gracias de que la mujer que lo va a dar a luz haya venido al mundo.

Aprender las doce fiestas es un modo de aprender el Evangelio en el orden en que la Iglesia lo canta. Esta dice: la salvación llega por una hija de Adán, no rodeándola.

challenges.title: The Exaltation of the Cross
challenges.summary: On September 14 the Church lifts up the cross and calls it the glory of Christ.
challenges.source: John 12:32 in the King James text, and the Church’s feast of September 14. Original prose.

lessons.heading: The cross held up
lessons.body:
The Exaltation of the Cross is kept on September 14. The Church remembers the finding of the cross in Jerusalem and the day it was lifted up so the people could see it. The hymn of the feast is not embarrassed by the wood. It treats the cross as the place where death was broken.

Jesus had already said, “And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me” (John 12:32). The evangelist adds that he said this signifying what death he should die. The feast takes him at his word. The lifting up is not an accident the Church explains away. It is the way he draws the world.

lessons.heading: A strict day
lessons.body: September 14 is kept as a fast day. The tone is not the tone of Pascha night. The Church can exalt the cross and still refuse to treat it as a charm. She stands in front of it, bows, and remembers that glory and suffering are not rivals in Christ.

lessonsEs.heading: La cruz levantada
lessonsEs.body:
La Exaltación de la Cruz se celebra el 14 de septiembre. La Iglesia recuerda el hallazgo de la cruz en Jerusalén y el día en que fue levantada para que el pueblo pudiera verla. El himno de la fiesta no se avergüenza de la madera. Trata la cruz como el lugar donde la muerte fue quebrada.

Jesús ya había dicho: “Y yo, si fuere levantado de la tierra, á todos traeré á mí mismo” (Juan 12:32, RV1909). El evangelista añade que esto decía “dando á entender de qué muerte había de morir” (Juan 12:33, RV1909). La fiesta lo toma al pie de la letra. El ser levantado no es un accidente que la Iglesia tenga que disimular. Es el modo en que Él atrae al mundo.

challenges.title: The Entrance of the Theotokos
challenges.summary: On November 21 the Church sings of Mary entering the temple and being prepared for the Annunciation.
challenges.source: The feast of November 21 in the Church’s calendar. Original prose. The Gospels do not narrate this entrance; the feast belongs to the Church’s received memory of Mary.

lessons.heading: Brought to the house of God
lessons.body:
The Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple is kept on November 21. The older account says Joachim and Anna brought their small daughter to the temple and that she grew up there in prayer. The Gospels do not tell that scene. The Church still keeps the feast, because the point is not a missing verse. The point is that the woman who will bear God was herself offered to God.

The temple in Jerusalem was the place of God’s presence among his people. Mary’s entrance says, in the Church’s poetry, that the living temple is being prepared. The child who walks in will become the one in whom the Word takes flesh.

lessons.heading: Between two feasts
lessons.body: November sits between Mary’s birth in September and Christ’s birth in December. The Entrance keeps the story from jumping. God does not arrive unannounced into a life that was never prayed. The feast asks the Church to offer her own children, and her own attention, to the same house of prayer.

choices: They do not narrate that scene

lessonsEs.heading: Llevada a la casa de Dios
lessonsEs.body:
La Entrada de la Theotokos en el Templo se celebra el 21 de noviembre. El relato más antiguo dice que Joaquín y Ana llevaron a su hija pequeña al templo y que ella creció allí en la oración. Los Evangelios no cuentan esa escena. La Iglesia igual guarda la fiesta, porque el punto no es un versículo que falta. El punto es que la mujer que va a dar a luz a Dios fue ella misma ofrecida a Dios.

El templo de Jerusalén era el lugar de la presencia de Dios entre su pueblo. La entrada de María dice, en la poesía de la Iglesia, que el templo vivo se está preparando. La niña que entra será aquella en quien el Verbo toma carne.

lessonsEs.body: Noviembre queda entre el nacimiento de María en septiembre y el nacimiento de Cristo en diciembre. La Entrada impide que la historia dé un salto. Dios no llega sin anuncio a una vida por la que nunca se oró. La fiesta le pide a la Iglesia que ofrezca a sus propios hijos, y su propia atención, a la misma casa de oración.

challenges.title: The Nativity of Christ
challenges.summary: On December 25 the Church confesses that the Word was born in Bethlehem.
challenges.source: Luke 2 in the King James text. Original prose on the feast of December 25.

lessons.heading: Born in the city of David
lessons.body:
The Nativity of Christ is kept on December 25. Luke says Mary “brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luke 2:7). The Church does not treat this as a soft legend beside the real theology. This is the theology: the Son of God has a birth, a body, and a town.

Angels speak to shepherds. The child is named Jesus. The feast lasts beyond a single morning because the Church is not finished looking at what happened. God has entered the world he made, from the inside.

lessons.heading: What the day is for
lessons.body: Christmas in the Church is preceded by a fast and followed by days that still sing the birth. The point of the feast is adoration, not a mood. The same child will be baptized, will teach, will be crucified, and will rise. December 25 is the day the Church refuses to start that story anywhere except in Mary’s arms.

lessonsEs.heading: Nacido en la ciudad de David
lessonsEs.body:
La Natividad de Cristo se celebra el 25 de diciembre. Lucas dice que María “parió á su hijo primogénito, y le envolvió en pañales, y acostóle en un pesebre, porque no había lugar para ellos en el mesón” (Lucas 2:7, RV1909). La Iglesia no trata esto como una leyenda suave al lado de la teología de verdad. Esta es la teología: el Hijo de Dios tiene un nacimiento, un cuerpo y una ciudad.

Los ángeles hablan a los pastores. Al niño se le pone por nombre Jesús. La fiesta dura más que una sola mañana porque la Iglesia no termina de mirar lo que pasó. Dios ha entrado en el mundo que hizo, desde adentro.

lessonsEs.body: La Navidad en la Iglesia va precedida de un ayuno y seguida de días que todavía cantan el nacimiento. El punto de la fiesta es la adoración, no un estado de ánimo. El mismo niño será bautizado, enseñará, será crucificado y resucitará. El 25 de diciembre es el día en que la Iglesia se niega a empezar esa historia en cualquier otro lugar que no sean los brazos de María.

challenges.title: Theophany, the Baptism of Christ
challenges.summary: On January 6 the Church stands at the Jordan, where the Trinity is shown.
challenges.source: Matthew 3:16–17 in the King James text. Original prose on the feast of January 6.

lessons.heading: The Jordan
lessons.body:
Theophany, also called Epiphany in the East, is kept on January 6. It is the baptism of Christ, not the visit of the magi. Matthew says the heavens were opened, the Spirit of God descended like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16–17).

The feast is called Theophany because God is shown: the Son in the water, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking. Jesus does not go to John because he needs washing from sin. He goes to take our washing on himself and to sanctify the waters.

lessons.heading: Water blessed
lessons.body: On this day the Church blesses water and the people drink it and carry it home. The act is not magic. It is a confession that the Jordan still reaches the font. Every baptism in the Church leans on this day. The beloved Son has already stood where the newly baptized will stand.

questions.prompt: Theophany on January 6 celebrates which event?
choices: The baptism of Christ

The Ascension
questions.explanation: January 6 is the Baptism of Christ, the showing of the Trinity at the Jordan.

lessonsEs.heading: El Jordán
lessonsEs.body:
La Teofanía, llamada también Epifanía en Oriente, se celebra el 6 de enero. Es el bautismo de Cristo, no la visita de los magos. Mateo dice: “he aquí los cielos le fueron abiertos, y vió al Espíritu de Dios que descendía como paloma, y venía sobre él. Y he aquí una voz de los cielos que decía: Este es mi Hijo amado, en el cual tengo contentamiento” (Mateo 3:16–17, RV1909).

La fiesta se llama Teofanía porque Dios se muestra: el Hijo en el agua, el Espíritu que desciende, el Padre que habla. Jesús no va a Juan porque necesite lavarse del pecado. Va para hacer suyo el lavado que nosotros necesitamos y para santificar las aguas.

challenges.title: The Presentation of Christ
challenges.summary: On February 2 the Church meets Simeon and Anna in the temple.
challenges.source: Luke 2:29–32 in the King James text. Original prose on the feast of February 2.

lessons.heading: Forty days
lessons.body:
The Presentation of Christ, sometimes called the Meeting, is kept on February 2, forty days after his birth. Luke says Mary and Joseph brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord. Simeon takes the child and says, “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: for mine eyes have seen thy salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

Simeon also says the child is “a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel” (Luke 2:32). Anna speaks of him to those who waited for redemption. The feast is the old Israel recognizing her Lord in a baby.

lessons.heading: A meeting, not a farewell
lessons.body: The candles of the day match Simeon’s word about light. The Church is not done with the temple. She is saying that the temple’s hope has arrived and can be held. Mary hears that a sword will pierce her soul. The meeting already leans toward the cross. Joy and that warning belong in the same chapter.

questions.prompt: Simeon says his eyes have seen what?
choices: Thy salvation
The end of Israel
A political treaty
questions.explanation: He says, “mine eyes have seen thy salvation.”

questions.prompt: The Presentation is kept how many days after the Nativity?
choices: Forty
Twelve
Three
questions.explanation: February 2 is the fortieth day.

lessonsEs.heading: Cuarenta días
lessonsEs.body:
La Presentación de Cristo, llamada a veces el Encuentro, se celebra el 2 de febrero, cuarenta días después de su nacimiento. Lucas dice que María y José lo llevaron a Jerusalén para presentarlo al Señor. Simeón toma al niño y dice: “Ahora despides, Señor, á tu siervo, conforme á tu palabra, en paz; Porque han visto mis ojos tu salvación” (Lucas 2:29–30, RV1909).

Simeón dice también que el niño es “Luz para ser revelada á los Gentiles, y la gloria de tu pueblo Israel” (Lucas 2:32, RV1909). Ana habla de Él a quienes esperaban la redención. La fiesta es el Israel antiguo reconociendo a su Señor en un bebé.

lessonsEs.body: Las velas del día coinciden con la palabra de Simeón sobre la luz. La Iglesia no ha terminado con el templo. El encuentro ya se inclina hacia la cruz. El gozo y ese aviso caben en el mismo capítulo.

challenges.title: The Annunciation
challenges.summary: On March 25 the Church hears Gabriel and Mary’s yes.
challenges.source: Luke 1:35 and 1:38 in the King James text. Original prose on the feast of March 25.

lessons.heading: The angel and the handmaid
lessons.body:
The Annunciation is kept on March 25, nine months before the Nativity. Gabriel tells Mary that the Holy Ghost will come upon her and the power of the Highest will overshadow her, “therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Mary answers, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word” (Luke 1:38).

The feast is the moment the incarnation is accepted, not merely predicted. God does not force the door. He speaks, and a woman of Israel consents. The Church has never treated that consent as a small courtesy.

lessons.heading: Often inside Lent
lessons.body: March 25 frequently falls in Great Lent. The Church does not postpone the feast until the fast is over. She keeps it, and the hymns hold the joy of the conception beside the penitence of the season. The child who is conceived will be the one who dies and rises. Lent is already his road.

questions.prompt: Luke 1:35 says the child will be called what?
choices: The Son of God
A son of Joseph only
The brother of John the Baptist by nature
questions.explanation: Gabriel says the holy one born of Mary shall be called the Son of God.

questions.prompt: Mary’s answer in Luke 1:38 begins with which words?
choices: Behold the handmaid of the Lord
I will not
Tell my cousins first
questions.explanation: She says, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.”

lessonsEs.heading: El ángel y la sierva
lessonsEs.body:
La Anunciación se celebra el 25 de marzo, nueve meses antes de la Natividad. Gabriel le dice a María: “El Espíritu Santo vendrá sobre ti, y la virtud del Altísimo te hará sombra; por lo cual también lo Santo que nacerá, será llamado Hijo de Dios” (Lucas 1:35, RV1909). María responde: “He aquí la sierva del Señor; hágase á mí conforme á tu palabra” (Lucas 1:38, RV1909).

La fiesta es el momento en que la encarnación es aceptada, no solo anunciada de antemano. Dios no fuerza la puerta. Habla, y una mujer de Israel consiente. La Iglesia nunca ha tratado ese consentimiento como una cortesía pequeña.

lessonsEs.body: El 25 de marzo cae con frecuencia en la Gran Cuaresma. La Iglesia no aplaza la fiesta hasta que termine el ayuno. La guarda, y los himnos sostienen el gozo de la concepción junto a la penitencia del tiempo. El niño que es concebido será el que muere y resucita. La Cuaresma ya es su camino.

challenges.title: The Entry into Jerusalem
challenges.summary: Palm Sunday opens Holy Week with the crowd’s hosanna and the road to the cross.
challenges.source: Matthew 21:9 in the King James text. Original prose on the movable feast of the Entry.

lessons.heading: Hosanna
lessons.body:
The Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem is one of the Twelve Great Feasts, and it moves with Pascha. Matthew says the crowds cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest” (Matthew 21:9). They cut branches. He rides a colt. The king arrives without an army.

The Church gives the people palms or pussy-willow branches and sings the same hosanna. She does not pretend the week will stay cheerful. The voices that bless him will soon be near the voices that accuse him. The feast tells the truth about both.

lessons.heading: The gate of Holy Week
lessons.body: Palm Sunday is the door, not the destination. The Bridegroom services, Thursday’s supper and the cross, Friday’s burial, and the night of Pascha all stand on the other side of this gate. To shout hosanna honestly is to follow him into the city, not to stop at the roadside.

questions.prompt: Matthew 21:9 has the crowds bless the one who comes in whose name?
choices: The name of the Lord
The name of Caesar
Their own name
questions.explanation: They cry, “Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.”

questions.prompt: The Entry into Jerusalem is timed by what?
choices: The date of Pascha
A fixed day in September
The winter solstice
questions.explanation: It is a movable feast, the Sunday that opens Holy Week.

lessonsEs.heading: Hosanna
lessonsEs.body:
La Entrada del Señor en Jerusalén es una de las Doce Grandes Fiestas, y se mueve con la Pascua. Mateo dice que las gentes aclamaban: “¡Hosanna al Hijo de David! ¡Bendito el que viene en el nombre del Señor! ¡Hosanna en las alturas!” (Mateo 21:9, RV1909). Cortan ramas. Él monta un pollino. El rey llega sin ejército.

La Iglesia da al pueblo palmas o ramas de sauce y canta el mismo hosanna. No finge que la semana se va a quedar alegre. Las voces que lo bendicen pronto estarán cerca de las voces que lo acusan. La fiesta dice la verdad de las dos.

lessonsEs.heading: La puerta de la Semana Santa
lessonsEs.body: El Domingo de Ramos es la puerta, no el destino. Los oficios del Esposo, la cena y la cruz del jueves, la sepultura del viernes y la noche de Pascua están del otro lado de esta puerta. Gritar hosanna de verdad es seguirlo hasta dentro de la ciudad, no detenerse a la orilla del camino.

challenges.title: The Ascension
challenges.summary: Forty days after Pascha, Christ ascends and does not abandon his body.
challenges.source: Acts 1:9–11 in the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: Taken up
lessons.body:
The Ascension is kept on the fortieth day after Pascha, always a Thursday. Acts says he was taken up and a cloud received him out of their sight. Two men in white ask why the disciples stand gazing: “this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

The feast is not an exit from the incarnation. The Son ascends with the humanity he took. Human nature is carried to the Father’s right hand. The Church does not say he left his body behind as a used garment.

lessons.heading: Waiting, not stranded
lessons.body: He tells them to wait for the promise of the Father. Ascension Thursday is ten days before Pentecost. The disciples return to Jerusalem and stay at prayer. The feast teaches the same posture: look up, and stay together until the Spirit comes. The one who ascended is the one who will come again.

questions.prompt: Acts 1:11 says Jesus will come again in what manner?
choices: In like manner as they saw him go
As a rumor only
Never
questions.explanation: The messengers say he shall come in like manner as they saw him go into heaven.

questions.prompt: The Ascension falls how many days after Pascha?
choices: Forty
Fifty
Seven
questions.explanation: It is the fortieth day, and Pentecost is the fiftieth.

lessonsEs.heading: Llevado arriba
lessonsEs.body:
La Ascensión se celebra el día cuadragésimo después de la Pascua, siempre un jueves. Hechos dice que, viéndolo ellos, “fué alzado; y una nube le recibió y le quitó de sus ojos” (Hechos 1:9, RV1909). Dos varones vestidos de blanco preguntan por qué los discípulos se quedan mirando: “este mismo Jesús que ha sido tomado desde vosotros arriba en el cielo, así vendrá como le habéis visto ir al cielo” (Hechos 1:11, RV1909).

La fiesta no es una salida de la encarnación. El Hijo asciende con la humanidad que tomó. La naturaleza humana es llevada a la diestra del Padre. La Iglesia no dice que dejó su cuerpo atrás como un vestido usado.

lessonsEs.heading: En espera, no varados
lessonsEs.body: Él les dice que esperen la promesa del Padre. El jueves de la Ascensión es diez días antes de Pentecostés. Los discípulos vuelven a Jerusalén y se quedan en oración. La fiesta enseña la misma postura: mira hacia arriba y quédate con los demás hasta que venga el Espíritu. El que ascendió es el que va a volver.

challenges.title: Pentecost
challenges.summary: On the fiftieth day the Spirit comes, and the Church begins to speak.
challenges.source: Acts 2:1–4 in the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: The upper room
lessons.body:
Pentecost is the fiftieth day after Pascha. Acts says they were all with one accord in one place. A sound came from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind. Cloven tongues like fire sat on each of them, and they were filled with the Holy Ghost and began to speak (Acts 2:1–4). The people outside hear the great works of God in their own languages.

The feast is the birth of the Church’s public preaching, not the invention of a new god. The Spirit is the same Spirit who rested on the Son at the Jordan. Now he rests on the body of disciples so that the world can hear.

lessons.heading: Kneeling, then standing
lessons.body: At vespers of Pentecost the Church kneels for the first time since Pascha and prays long prayers to the Spirit. The week after is free of fasting. The point of the day is not a private thrill. It is the Spirit making one people who can tell the truth about Christ in words their neighbors understand.

questions.prompt: Acts 2 says the disciples were filled with whom?
choices: The Holy Ghost
A spirit of fear only
The emperor’s genius
questions.explanation: They were filled with the Holy Ghost and began to speak.

questions.prompt: Pentecost is which day after Pascha?
choices: The fiftieth
The third
The twelfth
questions.explanation: Pentecost means the fiftieth day.

lessonsEs.heading: El aposento alto
lessonsEs.body:
Pentecostés es el día quincuagésimo después de la Pascua. Hechos dice: “estaban todos unánimes juntos”. “Y de repente vino un estruendo del cielo como de un viento recio que corría, el cual hinchió toda la casa donde estaban sentados”. “Y se les aparecieron lenguas repartidas, como de fuego, que se asentó sobre cada uno de ellos”. “Y fueron todos llenos del Espíritu Santo, y comenzaron á hablar en otras lenguas, como el Espíritu les daba que hablasen” (Hechos 2:1–4, RV1909). La gente de afuera oye las grandezas de Dios en sus propias lenguas.

La fiesta es el nacimiento de la predicación pública de la Iglesia, no la invención de un dios nuevo. El Espíritu es el mismo Espíritu que reposó sobre el Hijo en el Jordán. Ahora reposa sobre el cuerpo de los discípulos para que el mundo pueda oír.

lessonsEs.heading: De rodillas, y después de pie
lessonsEs.body: En las vísperas de Pentecostés la Iglesia se arrodilla por primera vez desde la Pascua y reza largas oraciones al Espíritu. La semana siguiente está libre de ayuno. El punto del día no es una emoción privada. Es el Espíritu haciendo un solo pueblo que puede decir la verdad sobre Cristo con palabras que sus vecinos entienden.

challenges.title: The Transfiguration
challenges.summary: On August 6 the Church sees Christ’s glory on the mountain before the cross.
challenges.source: Matthew 17:2–5 in the King James text. Original prose on the feast of August 6.

lessons.heading: Light on the mountain
lessons.body:
The Transfiguration is kept on August 6. Matthew says Jesus was transfigured before Peter, James, and John, “and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light” (Matthew 17:2). Moses and Elijah appear. A bright cloud overshadows them, and a voice says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him” (Matthew 17:5).

The feast shows that the one who will be crucified is already the beloved Son. The light is not a costume. It is his glory, briefly suffered to be seen so the disciples will not collapse when they see him on the cross.

lessons.heading: Fruit and the fast that follows
lessons.body: In many places grapes or other fruit are blessed on this day. Two days later the fast before the Dormition continues toward August 15. Glory and a short fast sit next to each other, as the mountain sits next to the road to Jerusalem. The voice on the mountain still gives the Church her instruction: hear him.

questions.prompt: Matthew 17:2 compares the shining of his face to what?
choices: The sun
A lamp in a tomb
The moon only
questions.explanation: His face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.

questions.prompt: The voice on the mountain says the disciples should do what?
choices: Hear him
Build three inns and stay
Forget Moses
questions.explanation: The voice says, “hear ye him.”

lessonsEs.heading: Luz en el monte
lessonsEs.body:
La Transfiguración se celebra el 6 de agosto. Mateo dice que Jesús se transfiguró delante de Pedro, Santiago y Juan, “y resplandeció su rostro como el sol, y sus vestidos fueron blancos como la luz” (Mateo 17:2, RV1909). Aparecen Moisés y Elías. Una nube de luz los cubre, y una voz dice: “Este es mi Hijo amado, en el cual tomo contentamiento: á él oid” (Mateo 17:5, RV1909).

La fiesta muestra que aquel que va a ser crucificado ya es el Hijo amado. La luz no es un disfraz. Es su gloria, dejada ver por un momento, para que los discípulos no se derrumben cuando lo vean en la cruz.

lessonsEs.heading: El fruto y el ayuno que sigue
lessonsEs.body: En muchos lugares se bendicen uvas u otra fruta en este día. Dos días después, el ayuno de antes de la Dormición sigue hacia el 15 de agosto. La gloria y un ayuno breve se sientan juntos, como el monte se sienta junto al camino a Jerusalén. La voz del monte sigue dándole a la Iglesia su instrucción: a Él oíd.

La gloria y un ayuno breve se sientan juntos, como el monte se sienta junto al camino a Jerusalén. La voz del monte sigue dándole a la Iglesia su instrucción: a Él oíd.

challenges.title: The Dormition of the Theotokos
challenges.summary: On August 15 the Church keeps Mary’s falling asleep and her place with her Son.
challenges.source: The feast of August 15. Luke 1:48 in the King James text. Original prose. The Gospels do not narrate Mary’s death.

lessons.heading: Falling asleep
lessons.body:
The Dormition is kept on August 15. Dormition means falling asleep. The Church believes Mary died as we die, and that her Son received her. The four Gospels do not describe that hour. The feast comes from the Church’s memory and her hymns, not from a verse that can be quoted as a news report.

What the Gospels do give is Mary’s own line: “For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). August 15 is one of those generations keeping the promise. Blessed does not mean exempt from the grave. It means God did not forget her there.

lessons.heading: The last of the great feasts
lessons.body: A short fast leads to the day. The cycle that began with her birth in September ends with her death in August, and then the year turns and begins again. The Church asks her prayers. She does not confuse the mother with the Son. She buries the mother in the hope of the resurrection he already accomplished.

questions.prompt: What does “Dormition” mean?
choices: Falling asleep
A military victory
The baptism of Christ
questions.explanation: Dormition is the falling asleep, the death, of the Theotokos.

questions.prompt: Luke 1:48 says all generations shall call Mary what?

questions.explanation: Mary says all generations shall call her blessed.

lessonsEs.heading: El quedar dormida
lessonsEs.body:
La Dormición se celebra el 15 de agosto. Dormición quiere decir quedar dormida. La Iglesia cree que María murió como morimos nosotros, y que su Hijo la recibió. Los cuatro Evangelios no describen esa hora. La fiesta viene de la memoria de la Iglesia y de sus himnos, no de un versículo que se pueda citar como una nota de prensa.

Lo que los Evangelios sí dan es la propia frase de María: “Porque ha mirado á la bajeza de su criada; porque he aquí, desde ahora me dirán bienaventurada todas las generaciones” (Lucas 1:48, RV1909). El 15 de agosto es una de esas generaciones cumpliendo la promesa. Bienaventurada no quiere decir exenta del sepulcro. Quiere decir que Dios no la olvidó allí.

La Iglesia pide sus oraciones. No confunde a la madre con el Hijo. Sepulta a la madre en la esperanza de la resurrección que Él ya realizó.
