challenges.title: Pascha
challenges.summary: Pascha is the feast of feasts: Christ is risen, and the fast breaks.
challenges.source: 1 Corinthians 15:20 and Mark 16:6 in the King James text. Original prose. Pascha is the center of the year and is named beside the Twelve Great Feasts.

lessons.heading: The night
lessons.body:
Pascha is not one feast among others. It is the feast that gives the others their meaning. The date moves with the first Sunday after the paschal full moon, and the whole year is counted from it: Lent before, Pentecost after, every Sunday as a small Pascha. At the door of the church the priest and people pass the news in a sentence: Christ is risen.

Paul writes, “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept” (1 Corinthians 15:20). The angel at the tomb says, “he is risen; he is not here” (Mark 16:6). The Church does not sing those lines as poetry that might be false. She sings them as the fact that judges every other fact.

lessons.heading: After the fast
lessons.body: The fast breaks. Eggs are dyed. The canon is long and the people stay. None of that replaces the announcement. If Christ is risen, death is no longer the last owner of a body. The Twelve Great Feasts tell his birth, his baptism, his cross, and his mother’s story. Pascha tells why any of those days are good news.

questions.prompt: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of whom?
choices: Them that slept
The angels only
The emperors
questions.explanation: 1 Corinthians 15:20 says he became the firstfruits of them that slept.

questions.prompt: How is the date of Pascha set?
choices: It moves; it is the Sunday after the paschal full moon
It is always March 1
It is always December 25
questions.explanation: Pascha is a movable feast, the first Sunday after the paschal full moon of the Church’s reckoning.

lessonsEs.heading: La noche
lessonsEs.body:
La Pascua no es una fiesta entre otras. Es la fiesta que les da sentido a las demás. La fecha se mueve con el primer domingo después de la luna llena pascual, y todo el año se cuenta desde ella: la Cuaresma antes, Pentecostés después, cada domingo como una Pascua pequeña. En la puerta de la iglesia el sacerdote y el pueblo se pasan la noticia en una frase: Cristo ha resucitado.

Pablo escribe: “Mas ahora Cristo ha resucitado de los muertos; primicias de los que durmieron es hecho” (1 Corintios 15:20, RV1909). El ángel junto al sepulcro dice: “resucitado há, no está aquí” (Marcos 16:6, RV1909). La Iglesia no canta esas líneas como poesía que podría ser falsa. Las canta como el hecho que juzga todo otro hecho.

lessonsEs.heading: Después del ayuno
lessonsEs.body: El ayuno se rompe. Se tiñen los huevos. El canon es largo y la gente se queda. Nada de eso reemplaza el anuncio. Si Cristo ha resucitado, la muerte ya no es la última dueña de un cuerpo. Las Doce Grandes Fiestas cuentan su nacimiento, su bautismo, su cruz y la historia de su madre. La Pascua dice por qué cualquiera de esos días es buena noticia.

challenges.title: How Great Lent is shaped
challenges.summary: Great Lent is forty days of fasting toward Pascha, with Holy Week as its own intense end.
challenges.source: The received order of Great Lent. Matthew 4:1–2 in the King James text. The Lenten prayer quoted is from Isabel Florence Hapgood, Service Book (1906), public domain.

lessons.heading: Forty days, then the week of the cross
lessons.body:
Great Lent is the fast before Pascha. It echoes the forty days Jesus was in the wilderness: “And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred” (Matthew 4:2). The Church counts forty days of fasting and then Holy Week, which is not a vague extra. Holy Week follows the supper, the trial, the cross, and the tomb one day at a time.

The weeks have their own memories. The Sunday of Orthodoxy, Gregory Palamas, the Cross, John Climacus, and Mary of Egypt lead to Palm Sunday. Forgiveness Vespers begins the fast with mutual pardon. Without that service, the fast is only a diet.

lessons.heading: A prayer for the road
lessons.body: The weekday services grow longer. The prayer of Ephraim is repeated with prostrations. In Hapgood’s public-domain text it begins, “O Lord and Master of my life, grant not unto me a spirit of slothfulness, of discouragement, of lust of power, of vain babbling.” The fast is aimed at those four, not at impressing anyone. It ends when the priest sings that Christ is risen and the people answer that he is risen indeed.

questions.prompt: Matthew 4:2 says Jesus fasted for how long?
choices: Forty days and forty nights
Three hours
A single sabbath
questions.explanation: He fasted forty days and forty nights.

questions.prompt: What begins Great Lent in the parish?
choices: Forgiveness Vespers
The Nativity liturgy
A wedding
questions.explanation: Forgiveness Vespers opens the fast with mutual pardon.

lessonsEs.heading: Cuarenta días, y después la semana de la cruz
lessonsEs.body:
La Gran Cuaresma es el ayuno antes de la Pascua. Hace eco de los cuarenta días que Jesús estuvo en el desierto: “Y habiendo ayunado cuarenta días y cuarenta noches, después tuvo hambre” (Mateo 4:2, RV1909). La Iglesia cuenta cuarenta días de ayuno y después la Semana Santa, que no es un extra vago. La Semana Santa sigue la cena, el juicio, la cruz y el sepulcro, un día a la vez.

Las semanas tienen sus propias memorias. El Domingo de la Ortodoxia, Gregorio Palamás, la Cruz, Juan Clímaco y María de Egipto conducen al Domingo de Ramos. Las Vísperas del Perdón empiezan el ayuno con el perdón mutuo. Sin ese oficio, el ayuno es solo una dieta.

lessonsEs.heading: Una oración para el camino
lessonsEs.body: Los oficios de entre semana se alargan. La oración de Efrén se repite con postraciones. En el texto de dominio público de Hapgood empieza: “Oh Señor y Dueño de mi vida, no me des un espíritu de pereza, de desaliento, de afán de poder, de vana palabrería”. El ayuno apunta a esas cuatro cosas, no a impresionar a nadie. Termina cuando el sacerdote canta que Cristo ha resucitado y el pueblo responde que en verdad ha resucitado.

challenges.title: Fasting without theater
challenges.summary: The Church fasts from certain foods, and Christ forbids turning that into a show.
challenges.source: Matthew 6:16–18 in the King James text. Original prose on the Church’s fast. Medical and pastoral exceptions belong to a priest, not to this page.

lessons.heading: What a fast is
lessons.body:
In Great Lent the Church asks the faithful to abstain from meat, dairy, and most days from fish, wine, and oil, with some days of relief marked on the calendar. The rule is older than any one parish kitchen. It is also not a contest. Children, the sick, the pregnant, and those whose work or poverty makes the full rule harmful should ask their priest rather than invent a private heroism or a private excuse.

Jesus says, “When ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance” (Matthew 6:16). Anoint the head, wash the face, and do not look like a person collecting credit. The Father who sees in secret is the audience that matters.

lessons.heading: Food is not the whole fast
lessons.body: A kitchen that is strict and a tongue that is cruel has missed the fast. The Church pairs the plate with prayer, alms, and fewer entertainments. Isaiah’s kind of fast, the one God recognizes, loosens burdens and feeds the hungry. The Lenten table is training for that, not a replacement for it. When Pascha comes, the same people who fasted are told to feast. Abstaining is for a season. Thanksgiving is the goal.

questions.prompt: Matthew 6:16 tells people who fast not to look like whom?
choices: The hypocrites, with a sad countenance
The angels
The apostles at Pentecost
questions.explanation: Jesus says not to fast like the hypocrites, who disfigure their faces to be seen.

questions.prompt: Who should adjust the fasting rule for illness or pregnancy?
choices: The person’s priest
A stranger on the internet
No one; the rule never bends
questions.explanation: The Church expects pastoral judgment. The sick and the pregnant ask their priest.

lessonsEs.heading: Qué es un ayuno
lessonsEs.body:
En la Gran Cuaresma la Iglesia pide a los fieles que se abstengan de carne, de lácteos y, la mayoría de los días, de pescado, vino y aceite, con algunos días de alivio marcados en el calendario. La regla es más antigua que la cocina de cualquier parroquia. Tampoco es un concurso. Los niños, los enfermos, las embarazadas y quienes por su trabajo o su pobreza harían daño con la regla completa deben preguntarle a su sacerdote, en vez de inventarse un heroísmo privado o una excusa privada.

Jesús dice: “Y cuando ayunáis, no seáis como los hipócritas, austeros” (Mateo 6:16, RV1909). “Mas tú, cuando ayunas, unge tu cabeza y lava tu rostro” (Mateo 6:17, RV1909), y no parezcas una persona que está cobrando crédito. El Padre que ve en secreto es el único público que importa.

lessonsEs.heading: La comida no es todo el ayuno
lessonsEs.body: Una cocina estricta y una lengua cruel se han perdido el ayuno. La Iglesia junta el plato con la oración, la limosna y menos entretenimientos. El ayuno que Dios reconoce, el de Isaías, desata las cargas y parte el pan con el hambriento. La mesa cuaresmal es entrenamiento para eso, no un reemplazo. Cuando llega la Pascua, a la misma gente que ayunó se le dice que haga fiesta. Abstenerse es por un tiempo. La acción de gracias es la meta.

challenges.title: Prayer, fasting, and alms
challenges.summary: Lent stands on three practices Jesus names together in the Sermon on the Mount.
challenges.source: Matthew 6 in the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: One sermon, three practices
lessons.body:
In Matthew 6 Jesus teaches alms, prayer, and fasting in a single stretch. He warns against doing any of them to be seen. He gives the words “Our Father.” He says to fast without a performance. The Church did not invent a three-part Lent and then hunt for a proof text. She found the three already standing together in the Sermon on the Mount.

Drop one and the other two warp. Prayer without fasting can stay in the head. Fasting without alms can turn into pride about a plate. Alms without prayer can become a way to manage God. Lent asks for all three, in secret where secret is possible, and in church where the body needs the body.

lessons.heading: A small rule
lessons.body: A workable Lent is concrete: a prayer morning and evening, the Jesus Prayer a few times a day, the fast your priest blesses, and one real gift of money or time to someone who needs it. Jesus says the Father who sees in secret shall reward openly (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18). The reward is not a reputation. It is the Father’s own attention, which was the point of the fast.

questions.prompt: Matthew 6 sets which three practices side by side?
choices: Alms, prayer, and fasting
Study, debate, and travel
Wealth, status, and ease
questions.explanation: The chapter teaches almsgiving, prayer, and fasting, each away from the eyes of admirers.

questions.prompt: Jesus says the Father sees the hidden work and will do what?
choices: Reward openly
Ignore it
Publish the giver’s name
questions.explanation: He says the Father who sees in secret shall reward thee openly.

lessonsEs.heading: Un sermón, tres prácticas
lessonsEs.body:
En Mateo 6 Jesús enseña la limosna, la oración y el ayuno en un solo tramo. Advierte que no se haga ninguna de las tres para ser visto. Da las palabras “Padre nuestro”. Dice que se ayune sin función. La Iglesia no inventó una Cuaresma de tres partes y después salió a buscar un texto de prueba. Encontró las tres ya de pie juntas en el Sermón del monte.

Suelta una y las otras dos se tuercen. La oración sin ayuno puede quedarse en la cabeza. El ayuno sin limosna puede volverse orgullo por un plato. La limosna sin oración puede volverse un modo de manejar a Dios. La Cuaresma pide las tres, en secreto donde el secreto es posible, y en la iglesia donde el cuerpo necesita al cuerpo.

lessonsEs.heading: Una regla pequeña
lessonsEs.body: Una Cuaresma que se puede vivir es concreta: una oración por la mañana y por la tarde, la oración de Jesús unas veces al día, el ayuno que tu sacerdote bendice, y un regalo real de dinero o de tiempo a alguien que lo necesita. Jesús dice que el Padre que ve en secreto te recompensará en público (Mateo 6:4, 6, 18, RV1909). La recompensa no es una reputación. Es la propia atención del Padre, que era el punto del ayuno.

challenges.title: Repentance is a road
challenges.summary: Repentance is turning around and walking home, not a single pang of regret.
challenges.source: Luke 15:18–20 in the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: I will arise
lessons.body:
The prodigal does not wait until he feels worthy. He says, “I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee” (Luke 15:18). Then he arises and goes. The father sees him a long way off and runs. Repentance in that story is a decision, a sentence, and a walk. The feeling of shame is real, and it is not the whole of it.

In the Church that walk has a place: confession before a priest, a canon of prayer if one is given, and communion when the priest says the person is ready. The point is not to linger in self-hatred. The point is to come home and stay.

lessons.heading: Again, without theater
lessons.body: People fall after they repent. The road includes getting up. John writes that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). Faithful means he does not tire of the truth told again. Just means forgiveness is not a shrug. It is the cross already borne. A Christian life is not a spotless record. It is a record of returns.

questions.prompt: In Luke 15:18 the son decides to tell his father what?
choices: I have sinned against heaven and before thee
I deserve the inheritance again
My brother was unfair
questions.explanation: He plans to say, “Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee.”

questions.prompt: 1 John 1:9 says that if we confess, God is what?
choices: Faithful and just to forgive
Indifferent
Obliged to ignore the sin
questions.explanation: He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us.

challenges.summaryEs: Arrepentirse es darse la vuelta y caminar a casa, no un solo pinchazo de pena.

lessonsEs.heading: Me levantaré
lessonsEs.body:
El hijo pródigo no espera a sentirse digno. Dice: “Me levantaré, é iré á mi padre, y le diré: Padre, he pecado contra el cielo, y contra ti” (Lucas 15:18, RV1909). Después se levanta y va. El padre lo ve desde lejos y corre. En esa historia el arrepentimiento es una decisión, una frase y una caminata. La vergüenza es real, y no es todo.

En la Iglesia esa caminata tiene un lugar: la confesión ante un sacerdote, un canon de oración si te lo dan, y la comunión cuando el sacerdote dice que la persona está lista. El punto no es quedarse en el odio a uno mismo. El punto es volver a casa y quedarse.

lessonsEs.body: La gente cae después de arrepentirse. El camino incluye levantarse. Juan escribe que si confesamos nuestros pecados, Dios es fiel y justo para perdonar (1 Juan 1:9). Fiel quiere decir que no se cansa de la verdad dicha otra vez. Justo quiere decir que el perdón no es un encogimiento de hombros. Es la cruz ya cargada. Una vida cristiana no es un expediente sin mancha. Es un expediente de regresos.

challenges.title: Alms that stay quiet
challenges.summary: Giving to the poor is part of the faith, and Jesus tells the giver not to advertise it.
challenges.source: Matthew 6:2–4 in the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: Do not sound a trumpet
lessons.body:
Jesus says, “When thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men” (Matthew 6:2). They have their reward already: they were seen. The other way is to give so quietly that the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. The Father who sees in secret is enough.

Alms are not a tip added to a spiritual life. In the Church they belong with prayer and fasting. Money, food, time, and attention all count when they actually reach a person in need. A gift that only decorates the giver is the trumpet Jesus names.

lessons.heading: Mercy has a direction
lessons.body: The early Church kept lists of widows and sent help when famine came. That habit is not optional nostalgia. James says faith without works is dead, and he names the works: visit the afflicted and refuse the world’s stain. Quiet giving is one of those works. It does not earn a place at the table. It shows that the person at the table has noticed who else is hungry.

questions.prompt: Matthew 6:2 says the hypocrites give alms in order to receive what?
choices: Glory of men
God’s secret reward
Nothing at all
questions.explanation: They give to have glory of men, and Jesus says they have their reward.

questions.prompt: Who sees the gift that was hidden?
choices: The Father
Only the recipient’s neighbors
No one
questions.explanation: The Father who sees in secret is the one who rewards.

challenges.summaryEs: Dar sin anuncio. La mano izquierda no necesita un discurso.

lessonsEs.heading: No hagas tocar trompeta
lessonsEs.body:
Jesús dice: “Cuando pues haces limosna, no hagas tocar trompeta delante de ti, como hacen los hipócritas en las sinagogas y en las plazas, para ser estimados de los hombres” (Mateo 6:2, RV1909). Ya tienen su recompensa: fueron vistos. El otro camino es dar tan en silencio que la izquierda no sepa lo que hace la derecha. El Padre que ve en secreto basta.

La limosna no es una propina añadida a una vida espiritual. En la Iglesia va junto con la oración y el ayuno. El dinero, la comida, el tiempo y la atención cuentan cuando de verdad llegan a una persona necesitada. Un don que solo adorna a quien da es la trompeta que Jesús nombra.

lessonsEs.heading: La misericordia tiene una dirección
lessonsEs.body: La Iglesia antigua guardaba listas de viudas y enviaba ayuda cuando venía el hambre. Ese hábito no es nostalgia opcional. Santiago dice que la fe sin obras está muerta, y nombra las obras: visitar a los afligidos y rechazar la mancha del mundo. Dar en silencio es una de esas obras. No se gana con ella un lugar en la mesa. Muestra que la persona que está en la mesa ha notado quién más tiene hambre.

challenges.title: Forgiveness before the fast
challenges.summary: The Lord’s Prayer ties God’s forgiveness to the forgiveness we give.
challenges.source: Matthew 6:12 and 6:14–15 in the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: As we forgive
lessons.body:
In the prayer Jesus taught, the Church says, “And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). He does not leave the line unexplained. “For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses” (Matthew 6:14–15).

This is not a bargain in which we purchase pardon. It is a warning that a clenched life cannot receive an open gift. Forgiveness may still tell the truth about harm. It refuses revenge. It refuses to keep the person as an enemy forever. Forgiveness Vespers at the start of Lent makes the whole parish practice the sentence out loud.

lessons.heading: A limit that is not a loophole
lessons.body: Forgiveness does not mean staying in reach of someone who is still dangerous. Safety and pardon are different acts. You can refuse revenge and still tell a priest, a family, or the proper authority what happened. What Jesus forbids is the nursed hatred that wants the other person damned. The Father’s forgiveness is the pattern: costly, clear, and aimed at restoration where restoration is possible.

choices: Our debtors

No one
questions.explanation: The prayer says, “as we forgive our debtors.”

questions.prompt: Matthew 6:15 says that if we do not forgive, what follows?
choices: The Father will not forgive our trespasses
Nothing changes
We are praised for strength
questions.explanation: Jesus says that if we forgive not, neither will the Father forgive our trespasses.

challenges.summaryEs: Perdonar es soltar la deuda, no fingir que no dolió.

lessonsEs.heading: Como nosotros perdonamos
lessonsEs.body:
En la oración que Jesús enseñó, la Iglesia dice: “Y perdónanos nuestras deudas, como también nosotros perdonamos á nuestros deudores” (Mateo 6:12, RV1909). Él no deja la frase sin explicar. “Porque si perdonareis á los hombres sus ofensas, os perdonará también á vosotros vuestro Padre celestial. Mas si no perdonareis á los hombres sus ofensas, tampoco vuestro Padre os perdonará vuestras ofensas” (Mateo 6:14–15, RV1909).

Esto no es un trato en el que compramos el perdón. Es un aviso de que una vida cerrada en un puño no puede recibir un don abierto. El perdón todavía puede decir la verdad sobre el daño. Se niega a la venganza. Se niega a guardar a la persona como enemiga para siempre. Las Vísperas del Perdón, al comienzo de la Cuaresma, hacen que toda la parroquia practique la frase en voz alta.

lessonsEs.heading: Un límite que no es una escapatoria
lessonsEs.body: Perdonar no quiere decir quedarte al alcance de alguien que sigue siendo peligroso. La seguridad y el perdón son actos distintos. Puedes negarte a la venganza y aun así decirle a un sacerdote, a la familia o a la autoridad que corresponde lo que pasó. Lo que Jesús prohíbe es el odio alimentado que quiere al otro condenado. El perdón del Padre es el modelo: costoso, claro, y apuntado a la restauración donde la restauración es posible.

challenges.title: Hospitality
challenges.summary: Receiving a stranger is one of the works the King names at the judgment.
challenges.source: Matthew 25:35 and Hebrews 13:2 in the King James text. Original prose.

lessons.heading: I was a stranger
lessons.body:
In the parable of the judgment the King says, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Matthew 25:35). The righteous do not remember doing it for him. He answers that what they did for the least of these, they did for him. Hospitality in that saying is not a hobby for people with large houses. It is one of the works by which the King recognizes his own.

Hebrews adds a reason that keeps the host humble: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2). Abraham’s table is in the background. So is the road to Emmaus, where the disciples knew the Lord in the breaking of bread. A meal can be a meeting.

lessons.heading: A door that can actually open
lessons.body: Hospitality can be a Sunday meal, a bed for a night, or a careful welcome of someone who does not yet know the prayers. It includes the people who are easy to overlook: the newcomer who stands at the back, the student far from home, the neighbor who is ashamed to ask. The Church’s coffee after liturgy is a small version of the same command, if it is real welcome and not a club. The King has already said which guest counts.

questions.prompt: In Matthew 25:35 the King says he was a stranger and the righteous did what?
choices: Took him in
Asked for his papers and shut the door
Ignored him politely
questions.explanation: He says, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in.”

questions.prompt: Hebrews 13:2 says some who welcomed strangers entertained whom unawares?
choices: Angels
Only relatives
No one of consequence
questions.explanation: The verse says some have entertained angels unawares.

challenges.summaryEs: Abrir la mesa es una forma antigua de tomar en serio al prójimo.

lessonsEs.heading: Fui huésped
lessonsEs.body:
En la parábola del juicio el Rey dice: “fuí huésped, y me recogisteis” (Mateo 25:35, RV1909). Los justos no recuerdan haberlo hecho por Él. Él responde que lo que hicieron por el más pequeño de estos, lo hicieron por Él. La hospitalidad en ese dicho no es un pasatiempo para gente de casas grandes. Es una de las obras por las que el Rey reconoce a los suyos.

Hebreos añade una razón que mantiene humilde a quien recibe: “No olvidéis la hospitalidad, porque por ésta algunos, sin saberlo, hospedaron ángeles” (Hebreos 13:2, RV1909). La mesa de Abraham está al fondo. También el camino a Emaús, donde los discípulos conocieron al Señor al partir el pan. Una comida puede ser un encuentro.

challenges.title: Visiting Each Other's Churches
challenges.summary: Two churches, one Lord. What a Pentecostal friend will see at the Liturgy, what an Orthodox friend will see at her service, and how to receive each other without sanding down what either of you believes.
challenges.source: Acts 2:42-47 · 1 Corinthians 14:26-40 · John 17:21 · Psalm 91

lessons.heading: Start where she actually stands
lessons.body: Karen is classical Pentecostal and Trinitarian: baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), filled with the Spirit, expecting God to move. That is not a half-Christianity waiting for your correction; it is a living faith since the day she gave her life to Christ. The first move in visiting each other's churches is honor. You do not have to pretend the differences are small. You do have to remember the person in the other pew is your sister before she is your debate topic.

lessons.heading: What she will see at the Liturgy
lessons.body: Prepare her gently. She will see icons, incense, chant, and a service that does not pause to explain itself. Tell her beforehand: nobody is worshipping paint; the Church surrounds its prayer with the faces of the witnesses (Hebrews 12:1). The center is the Eucharist, the true Body and Blood, received with fear and love. She does not have to receive to be welcome. Let her stand, watch, and pray as she can. A guest who is not pressured becomes a guest who can actually hear.

lessons.heading: What you will see at her service
lessons.body: Expect raised hands, loud praise, an altar call, and maybe tongues — Paul regulates tongues, he does not forbid them: let all things be done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40), and the one who speaks in a tongue should pray for the interpretation (14:13). Her church baptizes Trinitarian and preaches Christ crucified. You will hear testimony: what God did this week. Receive it as she means it. You can love the zeal in a room without adopting every claim made in it.

lessons.heading: Disagree like family
lessons.body: You will still disagree — on saints, on baptism, on what happens at the table. Her rule is a good one: disagree peacefully, never disrespectfully. Debate questions; never make the person feel small for asking them. The goal of visiting each other is not to win the other church. It is what Christ prayed the night before the Cross: that they all may be one, that the world may believe (John 17:21). Start with the Creed you share, the Scriptures you share, and the Savior you share. Let the rest be a long friendship, not a first date test.

questions.prompt: What is the first move when visiting each other's churches?
choices: Correct her doctrine in the parking lot
Honor: she is your sister before she is your debate topic
Pretend there are no differences at all
Rate her service against yours
questions.explanation: Honor comes first. You do not have to pretend the differences are small; you do have to remember she is your sister in Christ before she is a topic.

questions.prompt: How should you prepare a Pentecostal friend for the Liturgy?
choices: Tell her she must receive the Eucharist
Explain icons and the service beforehand, and let her stand and pray as she can
Say nothing and let her figure it out
Warn her the chanting is not worship
questions.explanation: A guest who is not pressured can actually hear. Explain the witnesses around the prayer (Hebrews 12:1); the center is the Eucharist, received by the faithful — she can be fully welcome without receiving.

questions.prompt: What does Paul actually do about tongues in 1 Corinthians 14?
choices: Forbids them outright
Regulates them: interpretation, order, decency (14:13, 40)
Says they ended before he wrote
Makes them the test of salvation
questions.explanation: Paul regulates tongues rather than forbidding them — interpretation and order. Her Trinitarian Pentecostal practice can be received on those terms without either of you lying about what you believe.

questions.prompt: John 17:21 — Christ's prayer the night before the Cross — asks the Father for what?
choices: That all churches use one building
That His people may be one, so the world may believe
That debates would stop forever
That visitors convert quickly
questions.explanation: That they all may be one, that the world may believe. Visiting each other serves that prayer; it is not a conversion trap.

questions.prompt: Her rule for disagreement — disagree peacefully, never disrespectfully — is best kept by…
choices: Debating the question without making the person feel small
Avoiding every hard topic forever
Winning quickly so it ends
Only texting, never face to face
questions.explanation: Debate questions; never make the person feel small for asking them. Peaceful disagreement is a discipline both churches claim to want.

questions.prompt: True or false: honoring her Pentecostal faith means you have to pretend the differences between your churches are small.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Honor is not pretending. You can hold real differences honestly and still receive her as a sister — that is the whole point of visiting rather than arguing from a distance.

questions.prompt: True or false: a guest at the Liturgy who does not receive the Eucharist can still be fully welcome.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: True. She can stand, watch, and pray as she can. Welcome does not require pressure, and pressure is the fastest way to close ears.

challenges.summaryEs: Dos iglesias, un solo Señor. Qué va a ver una amiga pentecostal en la Liturgia, qué va a ver un amigo ortodoxo en su culto, y cómo recibirse sin limar lo que cada uno cree.

challenges.title: Strong, and Still Cared For
challenges.summary: For the woman who has to be strong — seven days on receiving: Moses told to accept help, the man carried by friends, Ruth in the field, Mary at His feet. One small 'receive one thing today' practice each day.
challenges.source: Exodus 18:17-24 · Mark 2:1-12 · Ruth 2 · Luke 10:38-42 · Psalm 116:2 · Psalm 23 · John 15:16

lessons.heading: Day 1 · Moses had to be told
lessons.body: Jethro watched Moses judge the people from morning till evening and said the thing a strong person rarely hears: what you are doing is not good; you will wear yourselves out (Exodus 18:17-18). Moses — the man who split the sea — accepted help, appointed others, and the work got better, not weaker. Strength that cannot receive instruction is just exhaustion with good branding. Today: let one person carry one thing, and do not apologize for it.

lessons.heading: Day 2 · The man who never asked
lessons.body: In Mark 2, four friends tear open a roof and lower a paralyzed man in front of Jesus. Notice: the man never asks. His friends carry him, and Jesus, seeing their faith, forgives and heals him. Some healings God routes through people who refuse to wait for an invitation. If you cannot ask, let that be the prayer today: Lord, teach me to be carried. And thank Him for the carriers.

lessons.heading: Day 3 · Ruth receives
lessons.body: Ruth gleans behind the reapers, and Boaz orders his men to leave handfuls of grain on purpose (Ruth 2:15-16). She does not steal, beg, or perform worthiness. She receives what kindness placed in her path and brings it home to Naomi. Receiving is not taking. It is letting what was left for you actually reach you. What has God left in your field today that your strength keeps walking past?

lessons.heading: Day 4 · Mary receives, Martha serves
lessons.body: Martha served until service became resentment; Mary sat and received, and the Lord defended the receiver (Luke 10:38-42). He did not say serving is faithless. He said the one who receives Him first has chosen the good part. Before the next shift of caring for everyone else, sit for five minutes and only receive: one psalm, no phone, no fixing. Let Him be the one who serves you.

lessons.heading: Day 5 · Her verse
lessons.body: Because he turned his ear to me, I will call on him as long as I live (Psalm 116:2). The psalmist does not say God turned His ear because the prayer was strong. He turned His ear because He is God. Your call is not measured by how well you ask. Today the practice is small on purpose: ask Him — out loud — for one concrete thing you need, and let the asking itself be the obedience.

lessons.heading: Day 6 · The good part is rest
lessons.body: He makes me lie down in green pastures; He restores my soul (Psalm 23:2-3). Restoration is something done to the sheep, not achieved by her. The Shepherd leads, carries the tired one home on His shoulders (Luke 15:5), and calls that joy, not burden. Rest today is not quitting. It is agreeing with the Shepherd about who does the carrying.

lessons.heading: Day 7 · Chosen and wanted
lessons.body: You did not choose me, but I chose you (John 15:16). Before you ever learned to be strong, you were wanted — by the God who turned His ear, and He has a way of sending that same choosing through ordinary people who show up and stay. This week you practiced receiving in small pieces. Keep the pieces. Being cared for is not the reward for the strong. It is the portion of the beloved.

questions.prompt: What did Jethro tell Moses in Exodus 18?
choices: Refuse all help to stay pure
What you are doing is not good — you will wear out; appoint others
Work longer hours to prove faith
Send the people away
questions.explanation: Jethro told Moses he would wear himself and the people out, and Moses obeyed by appointing others. Accepting help made the work better, not weaker.

questions.prompt: In Mark 2, when Jesus saw the paralyzed man lowered through the roof, whose faith does the text name?
choices: The man's flawless asking
Their faith — the friends who carried him
The crowd blocking the door
Nobody's; it was automatic
questions.explanation: Seeing their faith (Mark 2:5). The man never asked. Some healings God routes through people who refuse to wait for an invitation.

questions.prompt: What did Boaz command his reapers in Ruth 2?
choices: Keep Ruth out of the field
Leave handfuls of grain on purpose for her
Charge her family for gleaning
Send her to another farm
questions.explanation: Boaz ordered handfuls left on purpose (Ruth 2:15-16). Ruth received what kindness placed in her path — receiving is not taking.

questions.prompt: In Luke 10, why did the Lord defend Mary over Martha?
choices: Serving is faithless
Receiving Him first is the good part that will not be taken away
Martha cooked badly
Guests should never be served
questions.explanation: He did not condemn serving; He said the one who receives Him first chose the good part (Luke 10:42).

questions.prompt: Psalm 116:2 — why does the psalmist say he will call on God as long as he lives?
choices: Because his prayers were strong
Because God turned His ear to him
Because he finally earned it
Because others stopped praying
questions.explanation: Because he turned his ear to me. God bends toward the caller; the call is not graded by how well you ask.

questions.prompt: Psalm 23:3 — who restores the sheep's soul?
choices: The sheep, by effort
He does — He restores my soul
The other sheep
Restoration is never needed
questions.explanation: He restores my soul. Restoration is done to the sheep, not achieved by her — the Shepherd carries, the sheep receives.

questions.prompt: John 15:16 — what does Christ say about being chosen?
choices: You chose yourselves by strength
You did not choose me, but I chose you
Only the strong are chosen
Being chosen must be earned yearly
questions.explanation: You did not choose me, but I chose you. Wanted comes before strong; being cared for is the portion of the beloved, not a prize.

challenges.title: Matthew 5–8 at Her Pace
challenges.level: 4 teaching cards · 8 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: The Sermon on the Mount and the healings that follow, in five-minute pieces with no streak to break. Built for the Saturday call: three questions, one memory verse, and the narrow road that is — literally — pressure.
challenges.source: Matthew 5-8 · Acts 14:22 · Psalm 91

lessons.heading: Five minutes, no debt
lessons.body: This path does not punish a hard week. Each piece is one small section of Matthew 5-8, and the only rule is: when you open it, you are exactly on time. Jesus taught crowds who had walked miles and worked all day; He did not hand them homework debt. Take the Beatitudes today, the Lord's Prayer tomorrow, the healings when you can. The Word keeps. So does He.

lessons.heading: The narrow road is pressure
lessons.body: In Matthew 7:14 the word for the narrow, hard road is thlipsis: pressure, affliction, being squeezed. The gate is not narrow because God is stingy with heaven. The road itself is pressure — and Acts 14:22 says it plainly: through many tribulations (thlipseon) we must enter the kingdom of God. If your week feels squeezed — shifts, a hurt child, no sleep — you are not off the road. By Christ's own word, the pressure is the road.

lessons.heading: Saturday question one: judging and discerning
lessons.body: Matthew 7 opens, Judge not, that ye be not judged — then a few verses later commands you to know teachers by their fruits (7:15-20). Both, in one chapter. Judging (krino) in the condemning sense means writing a person's final verdict, which belongs to God. Discerning means testing a teaching or a pattern by its fruit, which He commands. Saturday talk: where is the line between condemning a person and discerning a teaching in your real week?

lessons.heading: Saturday questions two and three
lessons.body: Two: if the narrow road is pressure, where has pressure actually brought you closer to God — not despite it, through it? Three: not everyone who says Lord, Lord (7:21) — so what does doing the Father's will look like on an ordinary Tuesday, on shift, at home with a little girl who needs you? Memory verse for the week: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find (Matthew 7:7). Pray the chapter like it was written for your Tuesday. It was.

questions.prompt: What does thlipsis, the word behind the narrow road in Matthew 7:14, actually mean?
choices: A tiny gate
Pressure, affliction, being squeezed
A secret password
A church building
questions.explanation: Thlipsis is pressure/affliction. The road is not narrow because God is stingy; the road itself is pressure (see Acts 14:22).

questions.prompt: Acts 14:22 says we enter the kingdom of God…
choices: When life gets easy
Through many tribulations
Only after perfect doctrine tests
By avoiding all pressure
questions.explanation: Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom. A squeezed week is not off the road — by Christ's word, the pressure is the road.

questions.prompt: Matthew 7 forbids judging and commands fruit-inspection in the same chapter. The distinction is…
choices: Never evaluate anything
Condemning a person is forbidden; discerning a teaching by its fruit is commanded
Judge people, never teachings
Only apostles may notice fruit
questions.explanation: Krino as condemning writes a final verdict on a person — God's job. Testing teaching by fruit (7:15-20) is commanded in the same breath.

questions.prompt: The memory verse of this path, Matthew 7:7, promises what to the one who asks and seeks?
choices: Instant wealth
Ask — it shall be given; seek — ye shall find; knock — it shall be opened
Silence from heaven
Only clergy are heard
questions.explanation: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.

questions.prompt: The house on the rock in Matthew 7:24-27 stands because the builder…
choices: Heard the words only
Heard the words and did them
Built fastest
Had the most money
questions.explanation: Whoever hears these sayings of mine and does them is like the wise man who built on the rock. Ordinary Tuesday obedience is the foundation.

questions.prompt: In Matthew 8, the centurion amazes Jesus because he…
choices: Offers a bribe
Trusts Christ's word alone — speak only the word, and my servant shall be healed
Demands a sign in the sky
Knows the Law best
questions.explanation: Speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed (Matthew 8:8). Jesus marvels: great faith trusts the word without needing to watch it work.

questions.prompt: True or false: missing days in this Matthew path means you have fallen behind and owe extra reading.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: False, by design. Five-minute pieces, no streak debt. When you open it, you are exactly on time.

questions.prompt: True or false: in Matthew 5, salt and light describe Christians hidden away from the world.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A city set on a hill cannot be hid, and the lamp goes on the stand (Matthew 5:14-15). Presence, not hiding.

challenges.title: Guarding the Senses
challenges.level: 4 teaching cards · 7 questions · Match the Word
challenges.summary: Her insight, in her framing: what comes in through the eyes shapes the soul. The lamp of the body, a covenant with the eyes, and a practical rule for phones, feeds, and a house with a little girl in it.
challenges.source: Matthew 6:22-23 · Job 31:1 · Psalm 101:3 · Philippians 4:8

lessons.heading: The insight, stated plainly
lessons.body: You said it first, and it is Orthodox to the bone: what comes in through the eyes shapes the soul. The senses are doors. Whatever we let stand in front of them long enough stops being entertainment and starts being formation — it teaches the heart what to want. Guarding the senses is not fear of the world. It is choosing what gets to raise you.

lessons.heading: The lamp of the body
lessons.body: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light (Matthew 6:22). Single here means undivided, honest, aimed at one thing. A divided eye — one eye on Christ, one eye feeding old hungers — fills the body with what Christ bluntly calls darkness (6:23). The Fathers read this as attention: the eye you keep is the light you live by.

lessons.heading: Job made a covenant
lessons.body: I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid? (Job 31:1). Job does not wait for temptation to negotiate. He settles the matter beforehand, in the calm, so the storm has nothing to bargain with. A covenant with the eyes is a decision made once that protects a thousand later moments: what you will not scroll, open, or keep on the screen — especially in a house where a little girl is learning what eyes are for.

lessons.heading: Fill the house with better light
lessons.body: Guarding is only half; the other half is filling. Whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure, lovely — think on these things (Philippians 4:8). David's version is household-shaped: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psalm 101:3). The practical rule for this week: one input fasted (the feed, the show, the old playlist) and one input feasted (a psalm at breakfast, the Saturday chapter open on the counter). Doors guarded, house lit.

questions.prompt: What does Christ call the eye in Matthew 6:22?
choices: A window to decorate
The light (lamp) of the body
A camera that only records
Unimportant to the soul
questions.explanation: The light of the body is the eye. If the eye is single, the whole body is full of light — attention is formation.

questions.prompt: Single eye in Matthew 6:22 means…
choices: Looking at one screen forever
Undivided, honest, aimed at one thing
Closing one eye in prayer
Refusing to read
questions.explanation: Single = undivided. A divided eye fills the body with darkness (6:23); a single eye fills it with light.

questions.prompt: Job 31:1 — what did Job make a covenant with?
choices: His servants
His eyes
His calendar
His enemies
questions.explanation: I made a covenant with mine eyes. He settled the matter beforehand, in the calm, so temptation had nothing to negotiate with.

questions.prompt: Psalm 101:3 puts the guarding of the eyes where?
choices: Only in church
In the house — I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes
Only for children
Only on fast days
questions.explanation: Household-shaped holiness: no wicked thing before the eyes at home either — where a little girl learns what eyes are for.

questions.prompt: Philippians 4:8 completes guarding with…
choices: Filling: think on what is true, honest, just, pure, lovely
Thinking about nothing at all
Only news and feeds
Guarding others instead
questions.explanation: Guarding is half; filling is the other half. Fast one input, feast on another — doors guarded, house lit.

questions.prompt: True or false: guarding the senses means fearing the world and hiding from it.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: False. It is choosing what gets to form you. The senses are doors, and whatever stands long before them starts teaching the heart what to want.

questions.prompt: True or false: a covenant with the eyes is decided once, beforehand, rather than renegotiated in every moment of temptation.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: True — that is Job's pattern. Settled in the calm, it protects a thousand later moments.

challenges.summaryEs: Tu propia idea, en tus palabras: lo que entra por los ojos forma el alma. La lámpara del cuerpo, un pacto con los ojos, y una regla práctica para el celular, las redes y una casa donde vive una niña.

games.title: Council map
games.summary: Match each doctrinal controversy to the council that gave a decisive answer.
prompts: The Son is not a creature; he is of one essence with the Father.
Mary is Theotokos because her Son is one divine Person incarnate.
Christ is one Person in two complete natures.
The veneration of icons is defended in light of the Incarnation.
explanations: Nicaea I (325) confessed the Son as homoousios — of one essence with the Father — and not a creature.
Ephesus (431) confessed Mary as Theotokos: the one born of her is the divine Son incarnate, one Person.
Chalcedon (451) confessed Christ as one Person in two complete natures, divine and human, without confusion.
Nicaea II (787) defended the veneration of icons because the Son truly became visible in the Incarnation.
games.summaryEs: Une cada controversia con el concilio que dio una respuesta clara.

games.title: Build the response
games.summary: Choose the strongest first move for each objection. Precision matters more than winning a point.
prompts: “If Jesus is God, why call Mary Mother of God?”
“If salvation is by grace, why talk about works?”
“If icons show Christ, are you worshipping wood?”
“If resurrection is real, was it just a return to ordinary mortal life?”
options: Distinguish veneration of an icon from worship due to God alone.
Identify the one born of Mary as the divine Son incarnate.
Distinguish glorified resurrection from ordinary resuscitation.
Explain how living faith bears the fruit of love through grace.
explanations: Theotokos names the Person Mary bore: the divine Son, who took flesh. It does not make Mary the source of the Godhead.
Grace and works are not rivals. Living faith bears the fruit of love; the work is the fruit of grace, not a wage that earns it.
An icon is venerated as a window to the person shown. The worship due to God alone is not given to wood.
The resurrection is a glorified life, not a return to ordinary mortal existence.
games.summaryEs: Elige el primer paso más firme ante cada objeción. La precisión importa más que ganar un punto.
